

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Air purifier
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Device that removes contaminants from the air in a room}}
An '''air purifier''' or '''air cleaner''' is a device which removes [[contaminant]]s from the air in a room to improve [[indoor air quality]]. These devices are commonly marketed to people with [[allergies]] or [[asthma]], and at reducing or eliminating [[passive smoking|second-hand tobacco smoke]].

Commercial grade air purifiers are manufactured as either small stand-alone units or larger units that can be affixed to an [[Air handler|air handler unit]] (AHU) or to an [[HVAC]] unit found in the medical, industrial, and commercial industries. Air purifiers may also be used in industry to remove impurities from air before processing. [[Pressure swing adsorption|Pressure swing adsorbers]] or other adsorption techniques are typically used for this.

Homemade, do-it-yourself air cleaners using [[Air filter|air filters]] are low-cost, high performance alternatives to commercial, stand-alone portable air cleaners.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Holder|first1=Amara L.|last2=Halliday|first2=Hannah S.|last3=Virtaranta|first3=Larry|date=2022|title=Impact of do-it-yourself air cleaner design on the reduction of simulated wildfire smoke in a controlled chamber environment|journal=Indoor Air|language=en|volume=32|issue=11|article-number=e13163|doi=10.1111/ina.13163|issn=1600-0668|pmc=9828579|pmid=36437679|bibcode=2022InAir..3241.R1H}}</ref>

==History==
In 1830, a patent was awarded to [[Charles Anthony Deane]] for a device comprising a copper helmet with an attached flexible collar and garment. A long leather hose attached to the rear of the helmet was to be used to supply air, the original concept being that it would be pumped using a double [[bellows]]. A short pipe allowed breathed air to escape. The garment was to be constructed from leather or airtight cloth, secured by straps.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Newton|first1=William|last2=Partington|first2=Charles Frederick|year=1825|title=Charles Anthony Deane - 1823 patent|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IwA1AAAAMAAJ|journal=Newton's London Journal of Arts and Sciences|publisher=W. Newton|volume=9|pages=341|access-date=May 9, 2021|archive-date=February 16, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216115329/https://books.google.com/books?id=IwA1AAAAMAAJ|url-status=live}}</ref>
In the 1860s, [[John Stenhouse]] filed two patents applying the absorbent properties of [[Charcoal|wood charcoal]] to air purification (patents 19 July 1860 and 21 May 1867), thereby creating the first practical [[respirator]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/dictionaryofnati54stepuoft/|title=Dictionary of National Biography|date=1898|publisher=[[Smith, Elder & Co.]]|editor-last=Lee|editor-first=Sidney|volume=54|location=[[London]]|pages=149|oclc=1070574795|access-date=May 9, 2021}}</ref>

In 1871, the physicist [[John Tyndall]] wrote about his invention, a fireman's respirator, as a result of a combination of protective features of the Stenhouse's respirator and other breathing devices.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tyndall|first=John|url=|title=Fragments of Science for Unscientific People: A series of detached essay, lectures and reviews|date=1871|publisher=[[Longman]]|location=[[London]]|oclc=1110295907}}</ref> This invention was later described in 1875.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=July 1875 |title=Fireman's Respirator |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2027/coo.31924080794518?urlappend=%3Bseq=168 |journal=[[The Manufacturer and Builder]] |volume=7 |pages=168–169 |access-date=May 9, 2021 |via=[[HathiTrust]] |hdl=2027/coo.31924080794518?urlappend=%3Bseq=168 |archive-date=July 1, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701042421/https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/imgsrv/html?id=coo.31924080794518&seq=171 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the 1950s, [[HEPA]] filters were commercialized as highly efficient [[air filter]]s, after being put to use in the 1940s in the United States' [[Manhattan Project]] to control airborne [[radioactive decay|radioactive]] contaminants.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ogunseitan|first=Oladele|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XtXJzogLCecC|title=Green Health: An A-to-Z Guide|date=June 28, 2011|publisher=[[SAGE Publishing]]|isbn=9781412996884|location=[[Thousand Oaks, California]]|pages=13|oclc=1089558597|access-date=May 9, 2021|archive-date=May 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210509142345/https://books.google.com/books?id=XtXJzogLCecC|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Gantz|first=Carroll|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QSNfCrpcSCAC&pg=PA128|title=The Vacuum Cleaner: A History|date=September 26, 2012|publisher=[[McFarland & Company]]|isbn=9780786493210|location=[[Jefferson, North Carolina]]|page=128|oclc=847028529|access-date=May 9, 2021|archive-date=May 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210509142345/https://books.google.com/books?id=QSNfCrpcSCAC&pg=PA128|url-status=live}}</ref>

The first residential HEPA filter was reportedly sold in 1963 by brothers Manfred and Klaus Hammes in Germany,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=White|first=Mason|date=May–June 2009|title=99.7 Per Cent Pure|journal=[[Architectural Design]]|volume=79|issue=3|pages=18–23|doi=10.1002/ad.883|issn=0003-8504}}</ref> who created the Incen Air Corporation which was the precursor to the [[IQAir]] corporation.<ref>{{cite web |title=The history of the air purifier – 11 steps to modern-day purifiers |url=https://housefresh.com/history-air-purifier/ |publisher=Housefresh |access-date=2026-01-06}}</ref>

==Use and benefits==
[[Dust]], [[pollen]], pet [[dander]], [[Mold (fungus)|mold]] [[spore]]s,<ref>{{cite web |last1=King |first1=Haldane |title=An Interview with Michael Rubino, The Mold Medic |url=https://molekule.com/blog/an-interview-with-michael-rubino-the-mold-medic/ |website=Molekule |date=9 September 2022 |access-date=6 October 2022 |archive-date=9 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209103253/https://molekule.com/blog/an-interview-with-michael-rubino-the-mold-medic/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[dust mite]] [[feces]] can act as [[allergens]], triggering [[allergies]] in sensitive people. Smoke [[particulate|particles]] and [[volatile organic compound]]s (VOCs) can pose a risk to health. Exposure to various components such as VOCs increases the likelihood of experiencing symptoms of [[sick building syndrome]].<ref name="ang">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Shaobin |last2=Ang |first2=H. M. |last3=Tade |first3=Moses O. |date=July 2007 |title=Volatile organic compounds in indoor environment and photocatalytic oxidation: State of the art |url= |journal=[[Environment International]] |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=694–705 |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2007.02.011 |issn=0160-4120 |pmid=17376530 |access-date= |via=[[Elsevier Science Direct]]}}</ref>

===COVID-19===
{{See also|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on public transport#Research and development|Corsi–Rosenthal Box}}
{{multiple image

Joseph Allen, director of the Healthy Buildings program at Harvard's School of Public Health, recommended in 2020 that school classrooms use an air purifier with a [[HEPA]] filter as a way to reduce transmission of COVID-19 virus, saying "Portables with a high-efficiency HEPA filter and sized for the appropriate room can capture 99.97 percent of airborne particles."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Daily|first=Laura|date=October 19, 2020|title=Can an air purifier help protect you against the coronavirus?|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/purifier-hepa-covid-particles-droplets/2020/10/16/1b54b27e-0f18-11eb-8a35-237ef1eb2ef7_story.html|url-access=limited|access-date=May 9, 2021|archive-date=January 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210107054314/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/purifier-hepa-covid-particles-droplets/2020/10/16/1b54b27e-0f18-11eb-8a35-237ef1eb2ef7_story.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

One fluid dynamic modelling study from 2021 suggests that operating air purifiers or air ventilation systems in confined spaces, such as an elevator, during their occupancy by multiple people leads to air circulation effects that could, theoretically, enhance viral transmission.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dbouk |first1=Talib |last2=Drikakis |first2=Dimitris |author-link2=Dimitris Drikakis |date=January 26, 2021 |title=On airborne virus transmission in elevators and confined spaces |journal=[[Physics of Fluids]] |location=[[Melville, New York]] |publisher=[[AIP Publishing]] |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=011905 |bibcode=2021PhFl...33a1905D |doi=10.1063/5.0038180 |issn=1070-6631 |oclc=1046236368 |pmc=7984422 |pmid=33790526}}</ref>  However, real-life testing of portable HEPA/UV air filters in COVID-19 wards in hospital demonstrated complete elimination of air-borne [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Conway Morris |first1=Andrew |last2=Sharrocks |first2=Katherine |last3=Bousfield |first3=Rachel |last4=Kermack |first4=Leanne |last5=Maes |first5=Mailis |last6=Higginson |first6=Ellen |last7=Forrest |first7=Sally |last8=Pereira-Dias |first8=Joana |last9=Cormie |first9=Claire |last10=Old |first10=Tim |last11=Brooks |first11=Sophie |date=2021-10-30 |title=The removal of airborne SARS-CoV-2 and other microbial bioaerosols by air filtration on COVID-19 surge units |journal=[[Clinical Infectious Diseases]] |volume=75 |issue=1 |language=en |pages=e97–e101 |doi=10.1093/cid/ciab933 |issn=1058-4838 |pmc=8689842 |pmid=34718446}}</ref> This report also showed a significant reduction in other bacteria, fungal and viral [[bioaerosol]], suggesting that portable filters such as this may be able to prevent not only [[nosocomial]] spread of [[COVID-19]] but also other [[hospital-acquired infection]]s.  Another study comparing paired wards with and without air purifying devices found an association between the deployment of air purifying devices and reduced nosocomial transmission of SARS-CoV-2, but the size of the effect and uncertainty around it were high.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Brock |first1=Rebecca C. |last2=Goudie |first2=Robert J.B. |last3=Peters |first3=Christine |last4=Thaxter |first4=Rachel |last5=Gouliouris |first5=Theodore |last6=Illingworth |first6=Christopher J.R. |last7=Morris |first7=Andrew Conway |last8=Beggs |first8=Clive B. |last9=Butler |first9=Matthew |last10=Keevil |first10=Victoria L. |date=October 2024 |title=Efficacy of Air Cleaning Units for preventing SARS-CoV-2 and other hospital-acquired infections on medicine for older people wards: A quasi-experimental controlled before-and- after study |journal=Journal of Hospital Infection |volume=155 |pages=1–8 |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.jhin.2024.09.017|doi-access=free |pmid=39374708 }}</ref> Acceptability of the devices in the hospital environment was imperfect,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Love |first1=Catriona |last2=Street |first2=Anna |last3=Riddell |first3=Edward |last4=Goudie |first4=Robert J.B. |last5=Brock |first5=Rebecca C. |last6=Thaxter |first6=Rachel |last7=Gouliouris |first7=Theodore |last8=Conway Morris |first8=Andrew |last9=Beggs |first9=Clive B. |last10=Peters |first10=Christine |last11=Butler |first11=Matthew J. |last12=Gould |first12=Dinah J. |last13=Keevil |first13=Victoria L. |date=September 2024 |title=Acceptability of Air Cleaning Units on Inpatient Wards: help for infection control or hindrance for ward occupants? |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0195670124003165 |journal=Journal of Hospital Infection |volume=155 |pages=254–256 |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.jhin.2024.09.010|pmid=39341284 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and as other restrictions such as masking and room occupancy were reduced so too did compliance with the air purifying devices.<ref name=":2" />

==Purifying techniques==
[[File:Fans by Dyson 1 2018-06-02.jpg|thumb|Air-purifiers with air flow generated by [[bladeless fan]]. Some models can act as heaters or [[humidifiers]] and may feature oscillation and adjustment of air flow angle (up and down).]]
[[File:パナソニック F-VX40H3 20160922.jpg|thumb|An air purifier placed under a table]]
There are two types of air purifying technologies, ''active'' and ''passive''. Active air purifiers release negatively charged ions into the air, causing pollutants to stick to surfaces, while passive air purification units use air filters to remove [[pollutant]]s. Passive purifiers are more efficient since all the [[dust]] and [[particulate matter]] is permanently removed from the air and collected in the filters.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 4, 2017|title=Best Air Purifiers: Why to Buy Air Purifier in India|url=https://www.kent.co.in/blog/best-air-purifiers-why-to-buy-air-purifier-in-india/|access-date=May 9, 2021|website=[[Kent RO Systems]]}}{{dead link|date=February 2024|bot=medic|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref>
Several different processes of varying effectiveness can be used to purify air. As of 2005, the most common methods were high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters and ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI).<ref>{{Cite journal|date=November 1, 2005|title=Air Cleaning Technologies|journal=[[Ontario Health Technology Assessment Series]]|publisher=Medical Advisory Secretariat|volume=5|issue=17|pages=1–52|issn=1915-7398|pmc=3382390|pmid=23074468|last1=Medical Advisory |first1=Secretariat }}</ref>

=== Filtration ===
[[Air filter]] purification traps airborne particles by size exclusion. Air is forced through a filter and particles are physically captured by the filter. Various filters exist notably including:
* High-efficiency particulate arrestance ([[HEPA]]) filters remove at least 99.97% of 0.3-micrometer particles and are usually more effective at removing larger and smaller particles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=da Roza |first=R. A. |date=December 1, 1982 |title=Particle size for greatest penetration of HEPA filters - and their true efficiency |url=https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/6241348-a5wL4J/ |journal=[[Office of Scientific and Technical Information]] |language=English |location=[[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] |doi=10.2172/6241348 |s2cid=129345954 |doi-access=free |osti=6241348 |access-date=May 10, 2021 |archive-date=May 16, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210516175118/https://www.osti.gov/biblio/6241348-a5wL4J/ |url-status=live }}</ref> HEPA purifiers, which filter all the air going into a [[clean room]], must be arranged so that no air bypasses the HEPA filter. In dusty environments, a HEPA filter may follow an easily cleaned conventional filter (prefilter) which removes coarser impurities so that the HEPA filter needs cleaning or replacing less frequently. HEPA filters do not generate ozone or harmful byproducts in the course of operation.
* Filter HVAC at [[Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value|MERV]] 14 or above are rated to remove airborne particles of 0.3 micrometers or larger. A high-efficiency MERV 14 filter has a capture rate of at least 75% for particles between 0.3 and 1.0 micrometers. Although the capture rate of a MERV filter is lower than that of a HEPA filter, a central air system can move significantly more air in the same period of time. Using a high-grade MERV filter can be more effective than using a high-powered HEPA machine at a fraction of the initial capital expenditure. Unfortunately, most furnace filters are slid in place without an [[hermetic seal|airtight seal]], which allows air to pass around the filters. This problem is worse for the higher-efficiency MERV filters because of the increase in [[drag (physics)|air resistance]]. Higher-efficiency MERV filters are usually denser and increase air resistance in the central system, requiring a greater [[air pressure]] drop and consequently increasing energy costs.
* There is ongoing research to enable viable and effective [[biocide]] treated air filters (i.e. air filters coated with antimicrobial agents) for preventing the spread of airborne pathogens.<ref>{{cite news |title=New antimicrobial air filters tested on trains rapidly kill SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses |url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2022-03-antimicrobial-air-filters-rapidly-sars-cov-.html |access-date=19 April 2022 |work=[[University of Birmingham]] |language=en |archive-date=19 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220419102216/https://medicalxpress.com/news/2022-03-antimicrobial-air-filters-rapidly-sars-cov-.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watson |first1=Rowan |last2=Oldfield |first2=Morwenna |last3=Bryant |first3=Jack A. |last4=Riordan |first4=Lily |last5=Hill |first5=Harriet J. |last6=Watts |first6=Julie A. |last7=Alexander |first7=Morgan R. |last8=Cox |first8=Michael J. |last9=Stamataki |first9=Zania |last10=Scurr |first10=David J. |last11=de Cogan |first11=Felicity |date=9 March 2022 |title=Efficacy of antimicrobial and anti-viral coated air filters to prevent the spread of airborne pathogens |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=2803 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.2803W |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-06579-9  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=8907282 |pmid=35264599}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Dae Hoon |last2=Joe |first2=Yun Haeng |last3=Piri |first3=Amin |last4=An |first4=Sanggwon |last5=Hwang |first5=Jungho |title=Determination of Air Filter Anti-Viral Efficiency against an Airborne Infectious Virus |journal=Journal of Hazardous Materials |date=5 September 2020 |volume=396 |article-number=122640 |doi=10.1016/j.jhazmat.2020.122640 |pmid=32339873 |pmc=7152926 |issn=0304-3894}}</ref>

=== Other methods ===
[[File:Baren B-757 air purifier.jpg|An air purifier which can use HEPA, ionization, PCO, UVGI, and ozone generation|thumb|right]]
* [[Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation]] - UVGI can be used to sterilize air that passes UV lamps via forced air.<ref name="u735">{{cite journal | last1=Li | first1=Xing | last2=Blatchley | first2=Ernest R. | title=Validation of In-Room UV-C-Based Air Cleaners | journal=Indoor Air | volume=2023 | date=2023-11-30 | issn=1600-0668 | doi=10.1155/2023/5510449 | doi-access=free | pages=1–14}}</ref> Air purification UVGI systems can be freestanding units with shielded UV lamps that use a fan to force air past the UV light. Other systems are installed in forced air systems so that the circulation for the premises moves micro-organisms past the lamps. Key to this form of sterilization is the placement of the UV lamps and a good filtration system to remove the dead micro-organisms. For example, forced air systems by design impede line-of-sight, thus creating areas of the environment that will be shaded from the UV light. However, a UV lamp placed at the coils and drain pan of the cooling system will keep micro-organisms from forming in these naturally damp places. The most effective method for treating the air rather than the coils is in-line duct systems, these systems are placed in the center of the duct and parallel to the airflow.
* [[Activated carbon]] is a [[porosity|porous]] material that can [[adsorption|adsorb]] volatile chemicals on a molecular basis, but does not remove larger particles. The adsorption process when using activated carbon must reach equilibrium thus it may be difficult to completely remove contaminants.<ref name="zeltner" /> Activated carbon is merely a process of changing contaminants from a gaseous phase to a solid phase, when aggravated or disturbed contaminants can be regenerated in indoor air sources.<ref name="lee">{{Cite journal|last1=Ao|first1=C. H.|last2=Lee|first2=S. C.|date=January 30, 2004|title=Combination effect of activated carbon with TiO<sub>2</sub> for the photodegradation of binary pollutants at typical indoor air level|journal=[[Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology]]|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|volume=161|issue=2–3|pages=131–140|doi=10.1016/S1010-6030(03)00276-4|issn=1010-6030|via=Elsevier Science Direct|hdl-access=free|hdl=10397/17192}}</ref> Activated carbon can be used at room temperature and has a long history of commercial use. It is normally used in conjunction with other filter technology, especially with HEPA. Other materials can also absorb chemicals but at a higher cost.
* Polarized-media electronic air cleaners use active electronically enhanced media to combine elements of both electronic air cleaners and passive mechanical filters. Most polarized-media electronic air cleaners use safe 24-volt DC voltage to establish the polarizing electric field. Most airborne particles have a charge and many are even bi-polar.  As airborne particles pass through the electric field the polarized field re-orients the particle to  adhere to a disposable fiber media pad. Ultra-fine particles (UFPs) that are not collected on their initial pass through the media pad are polarized and agglomerate to other particles, odor and VOC molecules and are collected on subsequent passes. The collection efficiency varies significantly by particle size.<ref name="collectionHVACFramework">{{cite journal | last1=Anandan | first1=Sudharshan | last2=Fix | first2=Andrew J. | last3=Freeman | first3=Andrew J. | last4=Miller | first4=Lance | last5=Scheg | first5=Devon P. | last6=Morgan | first6=Xavier | last7=Park | first7=Jae Hong | last8=Horton | first8=William T. | last9=Blatchley | first9=Ernest R. | last10=Warsinger | first10=David M. | title=Framework for assessing collection-based photocatalytic oxidation systems in HVAC applications for bioaerosol control | journal=Building and Environment | volume=261 | date=2024 | doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2024.111593 | article-number=111593}}</ref> The efficiency of polarized-media electronic air cleaners increases as they load, providing high-efficiency filtration, with air resistance typically equal to or less than passive filters. Polarized-media technology is non-ionizing, which means no ozone is produced.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 23, 2006|title=Polarized-Media EACs Are Coming Of Age|url=https://www.achrnews.com/articles/95615-polarized-media-eacs-are-coming-of-age|url-status=live|access-date=November 24, 2021|website=www.achrnews.com|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030082339/https://www.achrnews.com/articles/95615-polarized-media-eacs-are-coming-of-age |archive-date=2020-10-30 }}</ref>
* [[Photocatalysis|Photocatalytic oxidation]] (PCO) is an emerging technology in the HVAC industry.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Branson|first=David|date=April 2006|title=Photocatalysis - Considerations for IAQ-Sensitive Engineering Designs|url=https://www.automatedbuildings.com/news/apr06/articles/csg/060320110906csg.htm|journal=Engineered Systems|access-date=2021-11-24|archive-date=2021-11-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124142902/https://www.automatedbuildings.com/news/apr06/articles/csg/060320110906csg.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition to the prospect of Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) benefits, it has the added potential for limiting the introduction of unconditioned air to the building space, thereby presenting an opportunity to achieve energy savings over previous prescriptive designs. As of May 2009{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} there was no more disputable concern raised by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory data that PCO may significantly increase the amount of [[formaldehyde]] in real indoor environments.{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} As with other advanced technologies, sound engineering principles and practices should be employed by the HVAC designer to ensure proper application of the technology. [[Photocatalysis|Photocatalytic]] oxidation systems are able to completely oxidize and degrade organic contaminants. For example, Volatile Organic Compounds found low concentrations within a few hundred ppmv or less are the most likely to be completely oxidized.<ref name="zeltner">{{Cite journal|last1=Zeltner|first1=Walter A.|last2=Tompkins|first2=Dean T.|date=January 2005|title=Shedding light on photocatalysis|journal=[[ASHRAE Transactions]]|location=[[New York City]]|publisher=[[ASHRAE]]|volume=111|pages=523–534|issn=0001-2505}}</ref> PCO uses short-wave [[ultraviolet]] light (UVC), commonly used for [[sterilization (microbiology)|sterilization]], to energize the catalyst (usually titanium dioxide (TiO<sub>2</sub>)<ref>{{cite web|date=August 2009|title=Residential Air Cleaners: A Summary of Available Information|url=http://www.epa.gov/iaq/pdfs/residential_air_cleaners.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924061343/http://www.epa.gov/iaq/pdfs/residential_air_cleaners.pdf|archive-date=September 24, 2015|access-date=May 10, 2021|work=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|edition=2nd}}</ref>) and oxidize [[bacteria]] and [[virus]]es.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bono|first1=Nina|last2=Ponti|first2=Federica|last3=Carlo|first3=Puna|last4=Candiani|first4=Gabriele|date=February 25, 2021|title=Effect of UV Irradiation and TiO<sub>2</sub>-Photocatalysis on Airborne Bacteria and Viruses: An Overview|journal=Materials |volume=14|issue=5|page=1075|doi=10.3390/ma14051075|pmid=33669103|pmc=7956276|bibcode=2021Mate...14.1075B|doi-access=free}}</ref> PCO in-duct units can be mounted to an existing forced-air [[HVAC]] system. PCO is not a filtering technology, as it does not trap or remove particles. Like polarized electric media, the effectiveness of PCO approaches are highly dependent on particle size, and system geometries must be tailored accordingly.<ref name="collectionHVACFramework" />  PCO systems are sometimes coupled with other filtering technologies for air purification. UV sterilization bulbs must be replaced about once a year; manufacturers may require periodic replacement as a condition of [[warranty]]. Photocatalytic Oxidation systems often have high commercial costs.<ref name="zeltner" />
** A related technology relevant to air purification is photoelectrochemical oxidation (PECO) [[Photoelectrochemical oxidation]]. While technically a type of PCO, PECO involves electrochemical interactions among the catalyst material and reactive species (e.g., through emplacement of cathodic materials) to improve quantum efficiency; in this way, it is possible to use lower energy UVA radiation as the light source and yet achieve improved effectiveness.<ref>{{cite patent |country=US |number=US7063820B2 |status=patent |title=Photoelectrochemical air disinfection |pubdate=December 16, 2004 |fdate=June 16, 2003 |pridate=June 16, 2003 |inventor=Goswami Dharendra Yogi |invent1=Yogi, Goswami Dharendra |assign1=University of Florida Research Foundation, Inc. |url=https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/7a/17/e1/284f5f4a48bb4f/US7063820.pdf }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210510102854/https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/7a/17/e1/284f5f4a48bb4f/US7063820.pdf |date=May 10, 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Grabianowski |first1=Ed |title=Which Air Purifiers Are Ozone-Free? Comparing Ionizers, UV-C, and HEPA |url=https://molekule.science/which-air-purifiers-are-ozone-free-comparing-ionizers-uv-c-and-hepa/ |website=Molekule |date=16 January 2019 |access-date=8 June 2022 |archive-date=27 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220627000344/https://molekule.science/which-air-purifiers-are-ozone-free-comparing-ionizers-uv-c-and-hepa/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
* [[Air ionizer|Ionizer purifiers]] use charged electrical surfaces or needles to generate electrically charged air or gas [[ion]]s. These ions attach to airborne particles which are then [[electrostatic]]ally attracted to a charged collector plate. This mechanism produces trace amounts of [[ozone]] and other oxidants as by-products.<ref name="ang" /> Most ionizers produce less than 0.05 [[parts per million|ppm]] of ozone, an industrial safety standard. There are two major subdivisions: the fanless ionizer and fan-based ionizer. Fanless ionizers are noiseless and use little power, but are less efficient at air purification. Fan-based ionizers clean and distribute air much faster. Permanently mounted home and industrial ionizer purifiers are called [[electrostatic precipitator]]s.
* Plasma air purifiers are a form of ionizing air purifier. Instead of precipitating particles on a plate, they are primarily intended to destroy volatile organic compounds, bacteria, and viruses by chemical reactions with generated ions. While promising in laboratory conditions, their usefulness and safety has not been established in air purification.<ref>{{Cite web|date=July 2018|title=Residential Air Cleaners: A Technical Summary|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2018-07/documents/residential_air_cleaners_-_a_technical_summary_3rd_edition.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|edition=3rd|archive-date=March 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210319134631/https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2018-07/documents/residential_air_cleaners_-_a_technical_summary_3rd_edition.pdf}}</ref>
* Far-[[Ultraviolet|UVC]] air purification systems (under development).<ref>{{Cite web|title=New type of ultraviolet light makes indoor air as safe as outdoors|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/03/220323101249.htm|access-date=28 March 2022|date=25 March 2022|website=Science Daily|language=en-US|archive-date=28 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328163629/http://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/03/220323101249.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eadie |first1=Ewan |last2=Hiwar |first2=Waseem |last3=Fletcher |first3=Louise |last4=Tidswell |first4=Emma |last5=O'Mahoney |first5=Paul |last6=Buonanno |first6=Manuela |last7=Welch |first7=David |last8=Adamson |first8=Catherine S. |last9=Brenner |first9=David J. |last10=Noakes |first10=Catherine |last11=Wood |first11=Kenneth |title=Far-UVC (222 nm) efficiently inactivates an airborne pathogen in a room-sized chamber |journal=Scientific Reports |date=23 March 2022 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=4373 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-08462-z  |doi-access=free|pmid=35322064 |pmc=8943125 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.4373E |language=en |issn=2045-2322}}</ref>
* [[Immobilized Cell Technology|Immobilized cell technology]] removes microfine particulate matter from the air by attracting charged particulates to a bio-reactive mass, or bioreactor, which enzymatically renders them inert.
* [[Ozone generator]]s are designed to produce ozone and are sometimes sold as whole-house air cleaners. Unlike ionizers, ozone generators are intended to produce significant amounts of ozone, a strong [[oxidant]] gas which can oxidize many other chemicals. The only safe use of ozone generators is in unoccupied rooms, utilising "shock treatment" commercial ozone generators that produce over 3000&nbsp;mg of ozone per hour. Restoration contractors use these types of ozone generators to remove smoke odors after fire damage, musty smells after flooding, [[mold remediation|mold]] (including [[toxic mold]]s), and the stench caused by decaying flesh which cannot be removed by bleach or anything else except for ozone. However, it is not healthy to breathe ozone gas, and one should use extreme caution when buying a room air purifier that also produces ozone.<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 9, 2000|title=Air Cleaners Designed to Intentionally Generate Ozone (Ozone Generators)|url=http://envair.ca/common/pdf/ozone-questions-hcan.pdf|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=Environmental Air Cleaning Ltd.|publisher=[[Health Canada]]|archive-date=May 12, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210512084640/http://envair.ca/common/pdf/ozone-questions-hcan.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* [[Titanium dioxide]] (TiO<sub>2</sub>) technology - [[nanoparticles]] of TiO<sub>2</sub>, together with [[Limestone|calcium carbonate]] to neutralize any [[acid]]ic gasses that may be adsorbed, is mixed into slightly porous paint. [[Photocatalysis]] initiates the decomposition of airborne contaminants at the surface.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hogan|first=Jenny|date=February 4, 2004|title=Smog-busting paint soaks up noxious gases|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn4636-smog-busting-paint-soaks-up-noxious-gases/|url-status=live|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=[[New Scientist]]|language=|archive-date=March 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308203753/https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn4636-smog-busting-paint-soaks-up-noxious-gases/}}</ref>
* Thermodynamic sterilization (TSS) - This technology uses heat sterilization via a ceramic core with microcapillaries, which are heated to {{convert|200|°C}}. It is claimed that 99.9% of microbiological particles - bacteria, viruses, dust mite allergens, mold and fungus spores - are incinerated.{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} The air passes through the ceramic core by the natural process of [[convection|air convection]], and is then cooled using heat transfer plates and released. TSS is not a filtering technology, as it does not trap or remove particles.{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} TSS is claimed not to emit harmful by-products (although the byproducts of partial [[pyrolysis|thermal decomposition]] are not addressed) and also reduces the concentration of ozone in the atmosphere.{{citation needed|date=August 2019}}
* Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) Technology also known as "ROS Purifier" - There are 7 airborne ROS. Some are short-lived and some are long-lived. The five short-lived ones are going to be hydroxyl radical, Singlet Oxygen (dioxidene), Superoxide, Atomic Oxygen, Peroxynitrite (peroxynitrite). The two long-lived ROS ones are Hydrogen Peroxide – Gas Phased, and Ozone. Due to the long-lived Hydrogen Peroxide (gas phased) and with low levels of Ozone (30ppb - 50 ppb) It is very effective in killing pathogens that include mold, bacteria, viruses, and germs in the air and on surfaces and provide odor control. Unlike Ozone generators that produce a high amount of ozone that is used as "shock treatment" is only effective in empty rooms without people present whereas ROS (Reactive Oxygen Species) purifiers can be effective safely 24/7 while people are present when ozone is (30ppb - 50 ppb). ROS (Reactive Oxygen Species) has very effective long-distance surface treatment due to its output of ozone (30ppb - 50ppb) and Hydrogen Peroxide it has, unlike Titanium dioxide that produces 2 ROS which are Hydroxyl radicals and superoxide that are a very short distance on surface treatment.

==Consumer concerns==
Other aspects of some air cleaners are hazardous gaseous by-products from ozone-generating units,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Air Purifiers Fact Sheet {{!}} Environmental Health & Safety {{!}} UMass Amherst |url=https://ehs.umass.edu/air-purifiers-fact-sheet |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=ehs.umass.edu |archive-date=2023-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230504225300/https://ehs.umass.edu/air-purifiers-fact-sheet |url-status=live }}</ref> noise level, frequency of filter replacement, electrical consumption, and visual appeal. Ozone production is typical for air ionizing purifiers. A high concentration of ozone is dangerous, although most air ionizers produce low amounts, low rates of ozone reduce the effectiveness. A build up can cause detrimental health effects especially for vulnerable people.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Association |first=American Lung |title=Ozone |url=https://www.lung.org/clean-air/outdoors/what-makes-air-unhealthy/ozone |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=www.lung.org |language=en |archive-date=2023-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505121336/https://www.lung.org/clean-air/outdoors/what-makes-air-unhealthy/ozone |url-status=live }}</ref> The noise level of a purifier can often be obtained through a customer service department and is usually reported in [[decibel]]s (dB). The noise levels for most purifiers can vary and may be dependent on fan speed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Best Air Purifier Buying Guide |url=https://www.consumerreports.org/appliances/air-purifiers/buying-guide/ |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Consumer Reports |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-07-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701042411/https://www.consumerreports.org/appliances/air-purifiers/buying-guide/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Frequency of filter replacement and electrical consumption are the major operation costs for any purifier. There are many types of filters; some can be cleaned by water, by hand or by [[vacuum cleaner]], while others need to be replaced every few months or years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Air Purifiers and the Cost of Clean Air |url=https://www.consumerreports.org/air-purifiers/air-purifiers-and-the-cost-of-clean-air-a6152505326/ |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Consumer Reports |date=25 October 2019 |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-07-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701042418/https://www.consumerreports.org/appliances/air-purifiers/air-purifiers-and-the-cost-of-clean-air-a6152505326/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Sometimes suitable filters are only sold by the manufacturer for a high cost, some have DRM control so only replacement filters authorised by the manufacturer can be used.<ref>{{Cite web |last=By |date=2022-08-13 |title=Air Filter DRM? Hacker Opts Out With NFC Sticker |url=https://hackaday.com/2022/08/13/air-filter-drm-hacker-opts-out-with-nfc-sticker/ |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Hackaday |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505121334/https://hackaday.com/2022/08/13/air-filter-drm-hacker-opts-out-with-nfc-sticker/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the United States, some purifiers are certified as [[Energy Star]] and are [[efficient energy use|energy efficient]].

HEPA technology is used in portable air purifiers as it removes common airborne allergens. The [[United States Department of Energy|US Department of Energy]] has requirements manufacturers must pass to meet HEPA requirements. The HEPA specification requires removal of at least 99.97% of 0.3 micrometers airborne pollutants.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 2015 |title=Specification for HEPA Filters Used by DOE Contractors |url=https://www.standards.doe.gov/standards-documents/3000/3020-astd-2015/@@images/file |access-date=5 May 2023 |website=U.S. Department of Energy |archive-date=14 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231214193557/https://www.standards.doe.gov/standards-documents/3000/3020-astd-2015/@@images/file |url-status=live }}</ref> Products that claim to be "HEPA-type", "HEPA-like", or "99% HEPA" do not satisfy these requirements and may not have been tested in independent laboratories.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Morris |first=David |date=22 August 2020 |title=How to pick the right air purifier for coronavirus protection |url=https://fortune.com/2020/08/22/air-purifier-protect-from-covid-19-coronavirus/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200822175611/https://fortune.com/2020/08/22/air-purifier-protect-from-covid-19-coronavirus/#selection-721.0-721.175 |archive-date=22 August 2020 |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref>

Air purifiers may be rated on a variety of factors, including [[Clean Air Delivery Rate]] (which determines how well air has been purified); efficient area coverage; [[air changes per hour]]; energy usage; and the cost of the replacement filters. Two other important factors to consider are the length that the filters are expected to last (measured in months or years) and the noise produced (measured in [[decibel]]s) by the various settings that the purifier runs on. This information is available from most manufacturers.

==Potential ozone hazards==
As with other health-related appliances, there is controversy surrounding the claims of certain companies, especially involving [[air ioniser|ionic air purifiers]]. Many air purifiers generate some ozone, an energetic [[allotrope]] of three [[oxygen]] atoms, and in the presence of humidity, small amounts of [[nitrogen oxide|NO<sub>x</sub>]]. Because of the nature of the ionization process, ionic air purifiers tend to generate the most ozone.{{Citation needed|date=January 2011}} This is a serious concern because ozone is a [[criteria air pollutant]] regulated by health-related US federal and state standards. In a controlled experiment, in many cases, ozone concentrations were well in excess of public and/or industrial safety levels established by US Environmental Protection Agency, particularly in poorly ventilated rooms.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Britigan|first1=Nicole|last2=Alshawa|first2=Ahmad|last3=Nizkorodov|first3=Sergey A.|date=May 2006|title=Quantification of Ozone Levels in Indoor Environments Generated by Ionization and Ozonolysis Air Purifiers|journal=[[Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association]]|publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]]|volume=56|issue=5|pages=601–610|doi=10.1080/10473289.2006.10464467|issn=1096-2247|eissn=2162-2906|pmid=16739796|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Ozone can damage the lungs, causing chest pain, coughing, shortness of breath and throat irritation. It can also worsen chronic respiratory diseases such as asthma and compromise the ability of the body to fight respiratory infections—even in healthy people. People who have asthma and allergy are most prone to the adverse effects of high levels of ozone. For example, increasing ozone concentrations to unsafe levels can increase the risk of asthma attacks.<ref>{{cite web|date=March 21, 2016|title=Health Effects of Ozone in Patients with Asthma and Other Chronic Respiratory Disease|url=https://www.epa.gov/ozone-pollution-and-your-patients-health/health-effects-ozone-patients-asthma-and-other-chronic|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427194110/https://www.epa.gov/ozone-pollution-and-your-patients-health/health-effects-ozone-patients-asthma-and-other-chronic|archive-date=April 27, 2021|work=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|access-date=May 11, 2021}}</ref>

Due to the below average performance and potential health risks, [[Consumer Reports]] has advised against using ozone producing air purifiers.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=August 28, 2014|title=Ozone Generators that are Sold as Air Cleaners|url=https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/ozone-generators-are-sold-air-cleaners|url-status=live|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|language=|archive-date=May 2, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200502103703/https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/ozone-generators-are-sold-air-cleaners}}</ref> Some manufacturers falsely claim outdoor and indoor ozone are different.<ref name="what" /> Claims that these devices restore a hypothesized ionic balance are unsupported by science.<ref name="what">{{cite web |url=https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/what-are-ionizers-and-other-ozone-generating-air-cleaners |title=What are ionizers and other ozone generating air cleaners? |author=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] |date=April 3, 2024 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |archive-date=April 5, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240405131939/https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/what-are-ionizers-and-other-ozone-generating-air-cleaners |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Ozone]] generators are used by cleanup contractors on unoccupied rooms to oxidize and permanently remove smoke, mold, and odor damage, and are considered a valuable and effective industrial tool.<ref>{{Cite web|title=How Long To Wait After Using Ozone Generator?|date=10 December 2021|url=https://besthvacguys.com/how-long-to-wait-after-using-ozone-generator/|access-date=2021-12-21|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-12-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211221225912/https://besthvacguys.com/how-long-to-wait-after-using-ozone-generator/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, these machines can produce undesirable by-products.<ref name=":1" />

In September 2007, the California Air Resources Board announced a ban of indoor air cleaning devices which produce ozone above a legal limit. This law, which took effect in 2010, requires testing and certification of all types of indoor air cleaning devices to verify that they do not emit excessive ozone.<ref>{{cite act|type=Act|number=2276|date=September 29, 2006|title=AB-2276 Ozone: indoor air cleaning devices.|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=200520060AB2276|access-date=May 11, 2021|archive-date=September 5, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180905180008/http://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=200520060AB2276|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Air Cleaner Regulation (AB 2276)|url=https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/air-cleaners-ozone-products/air-cleaner-regulation-ab-2276|url-status=live|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=[[California Air Resources Board]]|archive-date=February 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217085441/https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/air-cleaners-ozone-products/air-cleaner-regulation-ab-2276}}</ref>

== Industry and markets ==
As of 2015, the United States residential air purifier total addressable market was estimated at $2 billion per year.<ref>{{Cite web|date=August 30, 2016|title=U.S. Residential Air Purifiers Market Poised to Surge from USD 2.02 Billion in 2015 to USD 2.72 Billion by 2021 – ZionMarketResearch.Com|url=https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2016/08/30/867910/0/en/U-S-Residential-Air-Purifiers-Market-Poised-to-Surge-from-USD-2-02-Billion-in-2015-to-USD-2-72-Billion-by-2021-ZionMarketResearch-Com.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190111070220/http://globenewswire.com/news-release/2016/08/30/867910/0/en/U-S-Residential-Air-Purifiers-Market-Poised-to-Surge-from-USD-2-02-Billion-in-2015-to-USD-2-72-Billion-by-2021-ZionMarketResearch-Com.html|archive-date=January 11, 2019|access-date=May 11, 2021|website=[[GlobeNewswire]]|publisher=}}</ref>

{{Short description|Activity that removes dirt and other particles from people, animals and objects}}{{pp-pc|small=yes}}

'''Cleaning''' is the process of removing unwanted substances, such as dirt, dust, and other impurities, from an object or environment.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=CDC |date=2024-03-11 |title=Cleaning |url=https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/disinfection-sterilization/cleaning.html |access-date=2025-10-31 |website=Infection Control |language=en-us}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=CDC |date=2025-03-18 |title=When and How to Clean and Disinfect Your Home |url=https://www.cdc.gov/hygiene/about/when-and-how-to-clean-and-disinfect-your-home.html |access-date=2025-10-31 |website=Water, Sanitation, and Environmentally Related Hygiene (WASH) |language=en-us}}</ref> Cleaning is often performed for [[beauty|aesthetic]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mack |first1=Robert C. |url=https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1739/upload/preservation-brief-01-cleaning-masonry.pdf |title=Preservation Brief 1: Assessing Cleaning and Water-Repellent Treatments for Historic Masonry Buildings |last2=Grimmer |first2=Anne |publisher=U.S. Department of the Interior - National Park Service |access-date=January 11, 2025}}</ref> [[hygiene|hygienic]], [[Function (engineering)|functional]], [[safety]], or [[environmental protection]] purposes. Cleaning occurs in many different physical contexts, and uses many different methods. Several occupations are devoted to cleaning.

==Contexts==
Cleaning occurs in various commercial, domestic, personal, and environmental contexts, which differ in scale and requirements.

* [[Commercial cleaning]], in business or other commercial settings
** [[Terminal cleaning]], in healthcare settings
* [[Housekeeping]], including [[spring cleaning]]<ref name=":1" />
* [[Hygiene]], including [[personal grooming]]
* [[Environmental remediation]], the removal of pollution or contaminants from the natural environment

==Methods==
[[File:Kulutusosuuskuntien Keskusliiton kokoelma D1974 7644 (30878351716).jpg|thumb|A shop assistant washing a shop window in [[Jyväskylä]], [[Finland]], in the 1960s]]
Cleaning is broadly achieved through mechanical action and/or [[chemical process]]es (usually [[solvation]]); many methods rely on a combination of mechanical and chemical action.<ref name=":0" /> Methods include:

* [[Washing]], usually done with water and often some kind of [[soap]] or [[detergent]]
** Mopping, usually using a [[mop]]
** Wiping, usually using a dry or moist piece of [[Textile#Cloth|cloth]] (such as [[toilet paper]], [[paper towel]] and [[wet wipe]])
** [[Pressure washing]], using a high-pressure stream of water
** [[Wet cleaning]], methods of professional laundering that avoid the use of chemical solvents
* [[Abrasive blasting]], typically used to remove bulk material from a surface, may be used to remove contaminants as well
* [[Acoustic cleaning]], the use of [[sound wave]]s to shake particulates loose from surfaces
** [[Ultrasonic cleaning]], using ultrasound, usually from 20 to 400&nbsp;kHz
** [[Megasonic cleaning]], a gentler mechanism than ultrasonic cleaning, used in [[Wafer (electronics)|wafer]], [[Implant (medicine)|medical implant]], and industrial part cleaning
* [[Carbon dioxide cleaning]], a family of methods for parts cleaning and sterilization using [[carbon dioxide]] in its various phases
* [[Dry cleaning]] of clothing and textiles, using a chemical solvent other than water
* [[Flame cleaning]] of structural steel, with an [[oxyacetylene]] flame
* [[Green cleaning]], using environmentally friendly methods and products
* [[Plasma cleaning]], using energetic [[plasma (physics)|plasma]] or dielectric barrier [[direct-current discharge|discharge]] plasma created from various gases
* [[Sputter cleaning]], performed in a vacuum by using physical [[sputtering]] of the surface
* [[Steam cleaning]], in both domestic and industrial contexts
* Sweeping, mechanical removal usually using a [[brush]]
* [[Thermal cleaning]], in industrial settings, involving [[pyrolysis]] and [[oxidation]]
* [[Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation]], which destroys [[microorganism]]s; used extensively in the medical and food industries
* Vacuum cleaning, using a [[vacuum cleaner]]

==Cleaning by item==
[[File:Conservation at the Church of Suceviţa.jpg|right|thumb|Surface cleaning in [[Conservation and restoration of cultural property|art conservation]]]]
[[File:Laundry in the river.jpg|thumb|[[Laundry]] in a river]]

Some items and materials require specialized cleaning techniques, due to their shape, size, location, or the material properties of the object and contaminants.<ref name=":1" />

===Buildings and infrastructure===
* [[Beach cleaning]]
* [[Carpet cleaning]]
* [[Modern chimney cleaning|Chimney cleaning]]
* [[Crime scene cleanup]]
* [[Exterior cleaning]]
