======================================================================
ARTICLE: Indoor air quality
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Air quality within and around buildings and structures}}
{{Use American English|date=April 2024}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=April 2024}}

[[File:Stacken 0c149d 1755.jpg|thumb|A dirty [[air filter]] being cleaned]]

{{Pollution sidebar|Air}}
'''Indoor air quality''' ('''IAQ''') is the [[air quality]] within [[building]]s and [[Nonbuilding structure|structure]]s. Poor indoor air quality due to '''indoor air pollution''' is known to affect the health, comfort, and well-being of building occupants. It has also been linked to [[Sick Building Syndrome|sick building syndrome]], respiratory issues, reduced productivity, and impaired learning in schools. Common pollutants of indoor air include [[Passive smoking|secondhand tobacco smoke]], [[Household air pollution|air pollutants from indoor combustion]], [[radon]], [[Mold health issues|molds]] and other [[allergen]]s, [[carbon monoxide]], [[volatile organic compound]]s, [[legionella]] and other bacteria, [[Asbestos|asbestos fibers]], [[carbon dioxide]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carroll |first1=GT|last2=Kirschman|first2=DL|last3=Mammana|first3=A |date=2022 |title= Increased CO2 levels in the operating room correlate with the number of healthcare workers present: an imperative for intentional crowd control |journal=Patient Safety in Surgery|volume=16 |issue=35|page=35 | doi=10.1186/s13037-022-00343-8|pmid=36397098 |pmc=9672642 |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[ozone]] and [[Atmospheric particulate matter|particulates]].

Source control, filtration, and the use of [[ventilation (architecture)|ventilation]] to dilute contaminants are the primary methods for improving indoor air quality. Although ventilation is an integral component of maintaining good indoor air quality, it may not be satisfactory alone.<ref>'' ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 62.1, Ventilation for Acceptable Indoor Air Quality'', ASHRAE, Inc., Atlanta, GA, US</ref> In scenarios where outdoor [[air pollution|pollution]] would deteriorate indoor air quality, other treatment devices such as [[Air filtration|filtration]] may also be necessary.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Belias |first1=Evangelos |last2=Licina |first2=Dusan |title=Outdoor PM2. 5 air filtration: optimising indoor air quality and energy |journal=Buildings & Cities |date=2022 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=186–203 |doi=10.5334/bc.153|doi-access=free }}</ref>

IAQ is evaluated through collection of air samples, monitoring human exposure to pollutants, analysis of building surfaces, and computer modeling of air flow inside buildings. IAQ is part of [[Green building#Indoor environmental quality enhancement|indoor environmental quality]] (IEQ), along with other factors that exert an influence on physical and psychological aspects of life indoors (e.g., lighting, visual quality, acoustics, and thermal comfort).<ref>{{cite web |last=KMC Controls|title=What's Your IQ on IAQ and IEQ?|date=September 24, 2015|url=https://www.kmccontrols.com/blog/whats-your-iq-on-iaq-ieq/ |access-date=April 12, 2021 |archive-date=April 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412190226/https://www.kmccontrols.com/blog/whats-your-iq-on-iaq-ieq/ |url-status=live }}{{unreliable source? |date=March 2024 }}</ref>

Indoor air pollution is a major health hazard in [[developing countries]] and is commonly referred to as "[[household air pollution]]" in that context.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bruce |first1=N |last2=Perez-Padilla |first2=R |last3=Albalak |first3=R |date=2000 |title=Indoor air pollution in developing countries: a major environmental and public health challenge. |journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization |volume=78 |issue=9 |pages=1078–92 |pmc=2560841 |pmid=11019457 }}</ref> But severe indoor air quality conditions also can emerge in affluent, highly-developed locales; for example, children fell sick from indoor mold in an apartment complex in [[Riviera Beach, Florida]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schlein |first1=Zach |title=Danger Inside: Children are Falling Sick at This South Florida Property |url=https://www.law.com/dailybusinessreview/2018/11/29/danger-inside-children-are-falling-sick-at-this-south-florida-property/ |access-date=28 July 2026 |work=Law.com |date=29 November 2018 |language=en }}</ref> Typically, poor indoor air quality is often related to cooking and heating methods by burning [[Biomass|biomass fuel]], in the form of [[wood]], [[charcoal]], [[Dry dung fuel|dung]], and [[crop residue]], in indoor environments that lack proper ventilation. Millions of people, primarily women and children, face serious health risks. In total, about three billion people in developing countries are affected by this problem. The [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) estimates that cooking-related indoor air pollution causes 3.8 million annual deaths.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 8, 2018 |title=Household air pollution and health: fact sheet |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/household-air-pollution-and-health |access-date=November 21, 2020 |website=WHO |language=en |archive-date=November 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211112161107/https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/household-air-pollution-and-health |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Global Burden of Disease Study|Global Burden of Disease]] study estimated the number of deaths in 2017 at 1.6 million.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ritchie |first1=Hannah |author1-link=Hannah Ritchie |last2=Roser |first2=Max |author2-link=Max Roser |date=2019 |title=Access to Energy |url=https://ourworldindata.org/indoor-air-pollution#indoor-air-pollution-is-one-of-the-leading-risk-factors-for-premature-death |journal=Our World in Data |access-date=April 1, 2021 |quote="According to the Global Burden of Disease study 1.6 million people died prematurely in 2017 as a result of indoor air pollution ... But it's worth noting that the WHO publishes a substantially larger number of indoor air pollution deaths.." |archive-date=November 1, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211101224356/https://ourworldindata.org/indoor-air-pollution#indoor-air-pollution-is-one-of-the-leading-risk-factors-for-premature-death |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Definition ==

Health depends on breathing clean air, free from chemicals and [[toxicant]]s as much as possible. It is estimated that humans spend approximately 90% of their lifetime indoors<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klepeis |first1=Neil E |last2=Nelson |first2=William C |last3=Ott |first3=Wayne R |last4=Robinson |first4=John P |last5=Tsang |first5=Andy M |last6=Switzer |first6=Paul |last7=Behar |first7=Joseph V |last8=Hern |first8=Stephen C |last9=Engelmann |first9=William H |title=The National Human Activity Pattern Survey (NHAPS): a resource for assessing exposure to environmental pollutants |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |date=July 2001 |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=231–252 |doi=10.1038/sj.jea.7500165 |pmid=11477521 |bibcode=2001JESEE..11..231K |osti=785282 |s2cid=22445147 |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc719357/ |access-date=March 30, 2024 |archive-date=March 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328171707/https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc719357/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and that indoor air pollution in some places can be much worse than that of the ambient air.<ref>U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Office equipment: design, indoor air emissions, and pollution prevention opportunities. Air and Energy Engineering Research Laboratory, Research Triangle Park, 1995.</ref><ref>U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Unfinished business: a comparative assessment of environmental problems, EPA-230/2-87-025a-e (NTIS PB88-127030). Office of Policy, Planning and Evaluation, Washington, DC, 1987.</ref>

Various factors contribute to high concentrations of pollutants indoors, ranging from influx of pollutants from external sources, [[Outgassing|off-gassing]] by furniture, furnishings including carpets, indoor activities (cooking, cleaning, painting, smoking, etc. in homes to using office equipment in offices), thermal comfort parameters such as temperature, humidity, airflow and [[Physicochemical properties|physio-chemical properties]] of the indoor air.{{Citation needed|date=March 2024}} Air pollutants can enter a building in many ways, including through open doors or windows. Poorly maintained air conditioners/ventilation systems can harbor mold, bacteria, and other contaminants, which are then circulated throughout indoor spaces, contributing to respiratory problems and allergies.

There have been many debates among indoor air quality specialists about the proper definition of indoor air quality and specifically what constitutes "acceptable" indoor air quality.

== Health effects ==

{{owidslider
|start   = 2021
|list    = Template:owidslider/indoor air pollution#gallery

IAQ is significant for human health as humans spend a large proportion of their time in indoor environments. Americans and Europeans on average spend approximately 90% of their time indoors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Klepeis |first1=Neil E |last2=Nelson |first2=William C |last3=Ott |first3=Wayne R |last4=Robinson |first4=John P |last5=Tsang |first5=Andy M |last6=Switzer |first6=Paul |last7=Behar |first7=Joseph V |last8=Hern |first8=Stephen C |last9=Engelmann |first9=William H |date=July 1, 2001 |title=The National Human Activity Pattern Survey (NHAPS): a resource for assessing exposure to environmental pollutants |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/7500165 |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |language=en |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=231–252 |doi=10.1038/sj.jea.7500165 |pmid=11477521 |bibcode=2001JESEE..11..231K |osti=785282 |issn=1559-0631 |access-date=November 13, 2023 |archive-date=November 13, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231113232225/https://www.nature.com/articles/7500165 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last= |first= |date=2014 |title=Combined or multiple exposure to health stressors in indoor built environments: an evidence-based review prepared for the WHO training workshop "Multiple environmental exposures and risks": 16–18 October 2013, Bonn, Germany |url=https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/350495 |journal=World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe |language=en |access-date=April 10, 2024 |archive-date=November 6, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231106192839/https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/350495 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) estimates that 3.2 million people die prematurely every year from illnesses attributed to indoor air pollution caused by indoor cooking, with over 237 thousand of these being children under 5. These include around an eighth of all global [[ischaemic heart disease]], [[stroke]], and [[lung cancer]] deaths. Overall the WHO estimated that poor indoor air quality resulted in the loss of 86 million [[Healthy Life Years|healthy life years]] in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 15, 2023 |title=Household air pollution |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/household-air-pollution-and-health |access-date=April 10, 2024 |website=World Health Organization |language=en |archive-date=November 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211112161107/https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/household-air-pollution-and-health |url-status=live }}</ref>

Studies in the UK and Europe show exposure to indoor air pollutants, chemicals and biological contamination can irritate the upper airway system, trigger or exacerbate asthma and other respiratory or [[cardiovascular]] conditions, and may even have carcinogenic effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Sierra N. |last2=Lam |first2=Holly C. Y. |last3=Goode |first3=Emma-Jane |last4=Marczylo |first4=Emma L. |last5=Exley |first5=Karen S. |last6=Dimitroulopoulou |first6=Sani |date=2 August 2023 |title=The Burden of Respiratory Disease from Formaldehyde, Damp and Mould in English Housing |journal=Environments |language=en |volume=10 |issue=8 |page=136 |doi=10.3390/environments10080136 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023Envi...10..136C |issn=2076-3298 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-11-16 |title=Chief Medical Officer (CMO): annual reports |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/chief-medical-officer-annual-reports |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=GOV.UK |language=en }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Project information {{!}} Indoor air quality at home {{!}} Quality standards {{!}} NICE |url=https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/indevelopment/gid-qs10113 |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=www.nice.org.uk }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The inside story: Health effects of indoor air quality on children and young people |url=https://www.rcpch.ac.uk/resources/inside-story-health-effects-indoor-air-quality-children-young-people |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=RCPCH |date=January 28, 2020 |language=en }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Halios |first1=Christos H. |last2=Landeg-Cox |first2=Charlotte |last3=Lowther |first3=Scott D. |last4=Middleton |first4=Alice |last5=Marczylo |first5=Tim |last6=Dimitroulopoulou |first6=Sani |date=15 September 2022 |title=Chemicals in European residences – Part I: A review of emissions, concentrations and health effects of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=839 |article-number=156201 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.156201 |pmid=35623519 |bibcode=2022ScTEn.83956201H |issn=0048-9697 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Literature review on chemical pollutants in indoor air in public settings for children and overview of their health effects with a focus on schools, kindergartens and day-care centres |url=https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/9789289055642 |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=www.who.int |language=en }}</ref>

Poor indoor air quality can cause [[sick building syndrome]]. Symptoms include burning of the eyes, scratchy throat, blocked nose, and headaches.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Burge |first1=P S |date=February 2004 |title=Sick building syndrome |journal=Occupational and Environmental Medicine |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=185–190 |doi=10.1136/oem.2003.008813 |pmc=1740708 |pmid=14739390 }}</ref>

=== Generated by indoor combustion ===

{{Main|Household air pollution}}

{{Further|Energy poverty and cooking}}

[[File:Tortillera_en_Guatemala.jpg|alt=a 3-stone stove|thumb|A traditional wood-fired 3-stone stove in Guatemala, which causes [[Indoor air pollution in developing nations|indoor air pollution]]]]
Indoor combustion, such as for cooking or heating, is a major cause of indoor air pollution and causes significant health harms and premature deaths. Hydrocarbon fires cause air pollution. Pollution is caused by both [[Biomass (energy)|biomass]] and [[fossil fuel]]s of various types, but some forms of fuels are more harmful than others.

Indoor fire can produce [[black carbon]] particles, [[NOx|nitrogen oxides]], [[Sulfur dioxide|sulfur oxides]], and [[Mercury (element)|mercury compounds]], among other emissions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Apte |first1=K |last2=Salvi |first2=S |title=Household air pollution and its effects on health. |journal=F1000Research |date=2016 |volume=5 |page=2593 |doi=10.12688/f1000research.7552.1 |pmid=27853506 |pmc=5089137 |quote=Burning of natural gas not only produces a variety of gases such as sulfur oxides, mercury compounds, and particulate matter but also leads to the production of nitrogen oxides, primarily nitrogen dioxide...The burning of biomass fuel or any other fossil fuel increases the concentration of black carbon in the air |doi-access=free }}</ref> Around 3 billion people cook over open fires or on rudimentary cook stoves. Cooking fuels are coal, wood, animal dung, and crop residues.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 7, 2020|title=Improved Clean Cookstoves|url=https://www.drawdown.org/solutions/improved-clean-cookstoves|access-date=December 5, 2020|website=Project Drawdown|language=en|archive-date=December 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215040740/https://www.drawdown.org/solutions/improved-clean-cookstoves|url-status=live}}</ref> IAQ is a particular concern in [[Developing country|low and middle-income countries]] where such practices are common.<ref>{{Cite book |title=WHO indoor air quality guidelines: household fuel combustion |publisher=World Health Organization |year=2014 |isbn=978-92-4-154888-5 |editor-last= |location=Geneva |editor-last2=}}</ref>

Cooking using [[natural gas]] (also called fossil gas, methane gas or simply gas) is associated with poorer indoor air quality. Combustion of gas produces [[nitrogen dioxide]] and carbon monoxide, and can lead to increased concentrations of nitrogen dioxide throughout the home environment which is linked to [[Respiratory disease|respiratory issues and diseases]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 November 2023 |title=Clearing the Air: Gas Cooking and Pollution in European Homes |url=https://www.clasp.ngo/research/all/cooking-with-gas-findings-from-a-pan-european-indoor-air-quality-field-study/ |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=CLASP |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Seals |first1=Brady |last2=Krasner |first2=Andee |title=Gas Stoves: Health and Air Quality Impacts and Solutions |url=https://rmi.org/insight/gas-stoves-pollution-health/ |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=RMI |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Carbon monoxide ====

{{Main|Carbon monoxide poisoning}}
One of the most acutely toxic indoor air contaminants is [[carbon monoxide]] (CO), a colorless and odorless gas that is a by-product of incomplete [[combustion]]. Carbon monoxide may be emitted from tobacco smoke and generated from malfunctioning fuel burning stoves (wood, kerosene, natural gas, propane) and fuel burning heating systems (wood, oil, natural gas) and from blocked [[flue]]s connected to these appliances.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Myers |first=Isabella |url=https://www.coresearchtrust.org/assets/uploads/images/CORT-Report-Medical-Examiners-Coroners-and-CO.pdf |title=The efficient operation of regulation and legislation: An holistic approach to understanding the effect of Carbon Monoxide on mortality |date=February 2022 |publisher=CO Research Trust}}</ref> In [[Developed country|developed countries]] the main sources of indoor CO emission come from cooking and heating devices that burn [[fossil fuel]]s and are faulty, incorrectly installed or poorly maintained.<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last1=Penney |first1=David |chapter=Carbon monoxide |date=2010 |title=WHO Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality: Selected Pollutants |chapter-url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK138710/ |access-date=March 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308140149/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK138710/ |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |url-status=live |publisher=World Health Organization |language=en |isbn=978-92-890-0213-4 |oclc=696099951 |last2=Benignus |first2=Vernon |last3=Kephalopoulos |first3=Stylianos |last4=Kotzias |first4=Dimitrios |last5=Kleinman |first5=Michael |last6=Verrier |first6=Agnes}}</ref> Appliance malfunction may be due to faulty installation or lack of maintenance and proper use.<ref name=":0" /> In [[Developing country|low- and middle-income countries]] the most common sources of CO in homes are burning [[Biofuel|biomass fuels]] and cigarette smoke.<ref name=":1" />

Health effects of [[Carbon monoxide poisoning|CO poisoning]] may be acute or chronic and can occur unintentionally or intentionally ([[self-harm]]). By depriving the brain of oxygen, acute exposure to carbon monoxide may have effects on the neurological system (headache, nausea, dizziness, alteration in consciousness and subjective weakness), the cardiovascular and respiratory systems ([[myocardial infarction]], shortness of breath, or rapid breathing, [[respiratory failure]]). Acute exposure can also lead to long-term neurological effects such as cognitive and behavioral changes. Severe CO poisoning may lead to unconsciousness, coma and death. Chronic exposure to low concentrations of carbon monoxide may lead to lethargy, headaches, nausea, flu-like symptoms and neuropsychological and cardiovascular issues.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 May 2022 |title=Carbon monoxide: toxicological overview |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/carbon-monoxide-properties-incident-management-and-toxicology/carbon-monoxide-toxicological-overview |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=UK Health Security Agency |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

The WHO recommended levels of indoor CO exposure in 24 hours is 4&nbsp;mg/m<sup>3</sup>.<ref name=":2">{{cite book |url=https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/345329/9789240034228-eng.pdf |title=WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide |date=2021 |publisher=World Health Organization |isbn=978-92-4-003422-8 |hdl=10665/345329 |hdl-access=free}}{{page needed|date=March 2024}}</ref> Acute exposure should not exceed 10&nbsp;mg/m<sup>3</sup> in 8 hours, 35&nbsp;mg/m<sup>3</sup> in one hour and 100&nbsp;mg/m<sup>3</sup> in 15 minutes.<ref name=":1" />

==== Secondhand tobacco smoke ====

{{Main|Passive smoking}}
[[Secondhand smoke]] is tobacco smoke which affects people other than the 'active' smoker. It is made up of the exhaled smoke (15%) and mostly of smoke coming from the burning end of the cigarette, known as [[sidestream smoke]] (85%).<ref name="pmid34963586">{{cite journal |last1=Soleimani |first1=Farshid |last2=Dobaradaran |first2=Sina |last3=De-la-Torre |first3=Gabriel E. |last4=Schmidt |first4=Torsten C. |last5=Saeedi |first5=Reza |date=March 2022 |title=Content of toxic components of cigarette, cigarette smoke vs cigarette butts: A comprehensive systematic review |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=813 |article-number=152667 |bibcode=2022ScTEn.81352667S |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.152667 |pmid=34963586}}</ref>

Secondhand smoke contains more than 7000 chemicals, of which hundreds are harmful to health.<ref name="pmid34963586" /> Secondhand tobacco smoke includes both a [[gas]]eous and a [[Particulates|particulate]] materials which, with particular hazards arising from levels of [[carbon monoxide]] and small particulates (fine particulate matter, especially [[Particulates#Size, shape, and solubility matter|PM2.5 and PM10]]) which get into the [[bronchiole]]s and [[Pulmonary alveolus|alveole]]s in the lung.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Considering smoking as an air pollution problem for environmental health &#124; Environmental Performance Index |url=http://archive.epi.yale.edu/the-metric/considering-smoking-air-pollution-problem-environmental-health |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180925172458/http://archive.epi.yale.edu/the-metric/considering-smoking-air-pollution-problem-environmental-health |archive-date=September 25, 2018 |access-date=March 21, 2018}}</ref> Inhaling secondhand smoke on multiple occasions can cause [[asthma]], [[pneumonia]], [[lung cancer]], and [[SIDS|sudden infant death syndrome]], among other conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arfaeinia |first1=Hossein |last2=Ghaemi |first2=Maryam |last3=Jahantigh |first3=Anis |last4=Soleimani |first4=Farshid |last5=Hashemi |first5=Hassan |date=June 12, 2023 |title=Secondhand and thirdhand smoke: a review on chemical contents, exposure routes, and protective strategies |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |volume=30 |issue=32 |pages=78017–78029 |bibcode=2023ESPR...3078017A |doi=10.1007/s11356-023-28128-1 |pmc=10258487 |pmid=37306877}}</ref>

[[Third-hand smoke|Thirdhand smoke]] (THS) refers to chemicals that settle on objects and bodies indoors after smoking. Exposure to thirdhand smoke can happen even after the actual cigarette smoke is not present anymore and affect those entering the indoor environment much later. Toxic substances of THS can react with other chemicals in the air and produce new toxic chemicals that are otherwise not present in cigarettes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arfaeinia |first1=Hossein |last2=Ghaemi |first2=Maryam |last3=Jahantigh |first3=Anis |last4=Soleimani |first4=Farshid |last5=Hashemi |first5=Hassan |date=June 12, 2023 |title=Secondhand and thirdhand smoke: a review on chemical contents, exposure routes, and protective strategies |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=30 |issue=32 |pages=78017–78029 |bibcode=2023ESPR...3078017A |doi=10.1007/s11356-023-28128-1 |issn=1614-7499 |pmc=10258487 |pmid=37306877}}</ref>

The only certain method to improve indoor air quality as regards secondhand smoke is to eliminate smoking indoors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Health |first=CDC's Office on Smoking and |date=May 9, 2018 |title=Smoking and Tobacco Use; Fact Sheet; Secondhand Smoke |url=https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/data_statistics/fact_sheets/secondhand_smoke/general_facts/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215040740/https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/data_statistics/fact_sheets/secondhand_smoke/general_facts/ |archive-date=December 15, 2021 |access-date=January 14, 2019 |website=Smoking and Tobacco Use |language=en-us}}</ref> Indoor [[Electronic cigarette|e-cigarette]] use also increases home [[particulate matter]] concentrations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fernández |first1=E |last2=Ballbè |first2=M |last3=Sureda |first3=X |last4=Fu |first4=M |last5=Saltó |first5=E |last6=Martínez-Sánchez |first6=JM |date=December 2015 |title=Particulate Matter from Electronic Cigarettes and Conventional Cigarettes: a Systematic Review and Observational Study. |journal=Current Environmental Health Reports |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=423–9 |doi=10.1007/s40572-015-0072-x |pmid=26452675 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2015CEHR....2..423F }}</ref>

==== Particulates ====

Atmospheric particulate matter, also known as [[particulates]], can be found indoors and can affect the health of occupants. Indoor particulate matter can come from different indoor sources or be created as secondary aerosols through indoor gas-to-particle reactions. They can also be outdoor particles that enter indoors. These indoor particles vary widely in size, ranging from nanomet (nanoparticles/ultrafine particles emitted from combustion sources) to micromet (resuspensed dust).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Vu |first1=Tuan V. |title=Indoor Air Pollution |last2=Harrison |first2=Roy M. |date=8 May 2019 |publisher=The Royal Society of Chemistry |isbn=978-1-78801-803-6 |editor-last=Harrison |editor-first=R. M. |publication-date=2019 |chapter=Chemical and Physical Properties of Indoor Aerosols |editor-last2=Hester |editor-first2=R. E.}}</ref> Particulate matter can also be produced through cooking activities. Frying produces higher concentrations than boiling or grilling and cooking meat produces higher concentrations than cooking vegetables.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abdullahi |first1=Karimatu L. |last2=Delgado-Saborit |first2=Juana Maria |last3=Harrison |first3=Roy M. |date=February 13, 2013 |title=Emissions and indoor concentrations of particulate matter and its specific chemical components from cooking: A review |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1352231013000861 |url-status=live |journal=Atmospheric Environment |language=en |volume=71 |pages=260–294 |bibcode=2013AtmEn..71..260A |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2013.01.061 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230521205004/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1352231013000861 |archive-date=May 21, 2023 |access-date=April 11, 2024}}</ref> Preparing a [[Thanksgiving dinner]] can produce high concentrations of particulate matter, exceeding 300 μg/m<sup>3</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Patel |first1=Sameer |last2=Sankhyan |first2=Sumit |last3=Boedicker |first3=Erin K. |last4=DeCarlo |first4=Peter F. |last5=Farmer |first5=Delphine K. |last6=Goldstein |first6=Allen H. |last7=Katz |first7=Erin F. |last8=Nazaroff |first8=William W |last9=Tian |first9=Yilin |last10=Vanhanen |first10=Joonas |last11=Vance |first11=Marina E. |date=June 16, 2020 |title=Indoor Particulate Matter during HOMEChem: Concentrations, Size Distributions, and Exposures |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=54 |issue=12 |pages=7107–7116 |bibcode=2020EnST...54.7107P |doi=10.1021/acs.est.0c00740 |issn=0013-936X |pmid=32391692 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Particulates can penetrate deep into the lungs and brain from blood streams, causing health problems such as [[Cardiovascular disease|heart disease]], [[Respiratory disease|lung disease]], [[cancer]] and [[preterm birth]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thangavel |first1=Prakash |last2=Park |first2=Duckshin |last3=Lee |first3=Young-Chul |date=2022-06-19 |title=Recent Insights into Particulate Matter (PM2.5)-Mediated Toxicity in Humans: An Overview |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |language=en |volume=19 |issue=12 |page=7511 |doi=10.3390/ijerph19127511 |doi-access=free |pmid=35742761 |pmc=9223652 |bibcode=2022IJERP..19.7511T |issn=1660-4601}}</ref>

=== Generated from building materials, furnishing and consumer products ===

{{See also|Building materials|Red List building materials}}

==== Volatile organic compounds ====

[[Volatile organic compound]]s (VOCs) include a variety of chemicals, some of which may have short- and long-term adverse health effects. There are numerous sources of VOCs indoors, which means that their concentrations are consistently higher indoors (up to ten times higher) than outdoors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=You |first1=Bo |last2=Zhou |first2=Wei |last3=Li |first3=Junyao |last4=Li |first4=Zhijie |last5=Sun |first5=Yele |date=November 4, 2022 |title=A review of indoor Gaseous organic compounds and human chemical Exposure: Insights from Real-time measurements |journal=Environment International |language=en |volume=170 |article-number=107611 |bibcode=2022EnInt.17007611Y |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2022.107611 |pmid=36335895 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Some VOCs are emitted directly indoors, and some are formed through the subsequent chemical reactions that can occur in the gas-phase, or on surfaces.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Weschler |first1=Charles J. |last2=Carslaw |first2=Nicola |date=March 6, 2018 |title=Indoor Chemistry |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.est.7b06387 |url-status=live |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=52 |issue=5 |pages=2419–2428 |bibcode=2018EnST...52.2419W |doi=10.1021/acs.est.7b06387 |issn=0013-936X |pmid=29402076 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231115234323/http://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.est.7b06387 |archive-date=November 15, 2023 |access-date=April 11, 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Carter-2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Carter |first1=Toby J. |last2=Poppendieck |first2=Dustin G. |last3=Shaw |first3=David |last4=Carslaw |first4=Nicola |date=January 16, 2023 |title=A Modelling Study of Indoor Air Chemistry: The Surface Interactions of Ozone and Hydrogen Peroxide |journal=Atmospheric Environment |language=en |volume=297 |article-number=119598 |bibcode=2023AtmEn.29719598C |doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2023.119598 |doi-access=free }}</ref> VOCs presenting health hazards include [[benzene]], [[formaldehyde]], [[tetrachloroethylene]] and [[trichloroethylene]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tsai |first1=Wen-Tien |date=March 26, 2019 |title=An overview of health hazards of volatile organic compounds regulated as indoor air pollutants |journal=Reviews on Environmental Health |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=81–89 |doi=10.1515/reveh-2018-0046 |pmid=30854833|bibcode=2019RvEH...34...81T }}</ref>

VOCs are emitted by thousands of indoor products. Examples include: paints, varnishes, waxes and lacquers, paint strippers, cleaning and personal care products, pesticides, building materials and furnishings, office equipment such as copiers and printers, [[correction fluid]]s and [[carbonless copy paper]], graphics and craft materials including glues and adhesives, permanent markers, and photographic solutions.<ref>{{cite web |date=August 5, 2010 |title=U.S. EPA IAQ – Organic chemicals |url=http://www.epa.gov/iaq/voc.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150909090046/http://www.epa.gov/iaq/voc.html |archive-date=September 9, 2015 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Epa.gov}}</ref> Chlorinated drinking water releases chloroform when hot water is used in the home. Benzene is emitted from fuel stored in attached garages.

Human activities such as cooking and cleaning can also emit VOCs.<ref name="pmid37609942">{{Cite journal |last1=Davies |first1=Helen L. |last2=O'Leary |first2=Catherine |last3=Dillon |first3=Terry |last4=Shaw |first4=David R. |last5=Shaw |first5=Marvin |last6=Mehra |first6=Archit |last7=Phillips |first7=Gavin |last8=Carslaw |first8=Nicola |date=August 14, 2023 |title=A measurement and modelling investigation of the indoor air chemistry following cooking activities |journal=Environmental Science: Processes & Impacts |language=en |volume=25 |issue=9 |pages=1532–1548 |doi=10.1039/D3EM00167A |issn=2050-7887 |pmid=37609942|doi-access=free |hdl=10034/628005 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="pmid38258874">{{Cite journal |last1=Harding-Smith |first1=Ellen |last2=Shaw |first2=David R. |last3=Shaw |first3=Marvin |last4=Dillon |first4=Terry J. |last5=Carslaw |first5=Nicola |date=January 23, 2024 |title=Does green mean clean? Volatile organic emissions from regular versus green cleaning products |journal=Environmental Science: Processes & Impacts |language=en |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=436–450 |doi=10.1039/D3EM00439B |issn=2050-7887 |pmid=38258874|doi-access=free }}</ref> Cooking can release long-chain [[aldehyde]]s and [[alkane]]s when oil is heated and [[terpene]]s can be released when spices are prepared and/or cooked.<ref name="pmid37609942" /> Leaks of natural gas from cooking appliances have been linked to elevated levels of VOCs including [[benzene]] in homes in the USA.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lebel |first1=Eric D. |last2=Michanowicz |first2=Drew R. |last3=Bilsback |first3=Kelsey R. |last4=Hill |first4=Lee Ann L. |last5=Goldman |first5=Jackson S. W. |last6=Domen |first6=Jeremy K. |last7=Jaeger |first7=Jessie M. |last8=Ruiz |first8=Angélica |last9=Shonkoff |first9=Seth B. C. |date=2022-11-15 |title=Composition, Emissions, and Air Quality Impacts of Hazardous Air Pollutants in Unburned Natural Gas from Residential Stoves in California |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=56 |issue=22 |pages=15828–15838 |doi=10.1021/acs.est.2c02581 |issn=0013-936X |pmc=9671046 |pmid=36263944|bibcode=2022EnST...5615828L }}</ref> Cleaning products contain a range of VOCs, including [[monoterpene]]s, [[sesquiterpene]]s, alcohols and [[ester]]s. Once released into the air, VOCs can undergo reactions with ozone and [[hydroxyl radical]]s to produce other VOCs, such as formaldehyde.<ref name="pmid38258874" />

Health effects include eye, nose, and [[throat irritation]]; [[headache]]s, loss of coordination, [[nausea]]; and [[Liver damage|damage to the liver]], kidney, and [[Neurotoxicity|central nervous system]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2014-08-18 |title=Volatile Organic Compounds' Impact on Indoor Air Quality |url=https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/volatile-organic-compounds-impact-indoor-air-quality |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=United States Environmental Protection Agency |language=en}}</ref>

Testing emissions from building materials used indoors has become increasingly common for floor coverings, paints, and many other important indoor building materials and finishes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 21, 2013 |title=About VOCs |url=http://cal-iaq.org/separator/voc/about-vocs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121181543/http://cal-iaq.org/separator/voc/about-vocs |archive-date=January 21, 2013 |access-date=September 16, 2019}}</ref> Indoor materials such as gypsum boards or carpet act as VOC 'sinks', by trapping VOC vapors for extended periods of time, and releasing them by [[outgassing]]. The VOCs can also undergo transformation at the surface through interaction with ozone.<ref name="Carter-2023" /> In both cases, these delayed emissions can result in chronic and low-level exposures to VOCs.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Oanh |first1=Nguyen Thi Kim |title=Advanced Air and Noise Pollution Control |last2=Hung |first2=Yung-Tse |date=2005 |isbn=978-1-58829-359-6 |series=Handbook of Environmental Engineering |volume=2 |pages=237–272 |chapter=Indoor Air Pollution Control |doi=10.1007/978-1-59259-779-6_7 }}</ref>

Several initiatives aim to reduce indoor air contamination by limiting VOC emissions from products. There are regulations in France and in Germany, and numerous voluntary ecolabels and rating systems containing low VOC emissions criteria such as EMICODE,<ref>{{cite web |title=Emicode |url=http://www.eurofins.com/emicode.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924003316/http://www.eurofins.com/emicode.aspx |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Eurofins.com}}</ref> M1,<ref>{{cite web |title=M1 |url=http://www.eurofins.com/m1.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924003357/http://www.eurofins.com/m1.aspx |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Eurofins.com}}</ref> [[Blue Angel (certification)|Blue Angel]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Blue Angel |url=http://www.eurofins.com/blue-angel.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924003302/http://www.eurofins.com/blue-angel.aspx |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Eurofins.com }}</ref> and Indoor Air Comfort<ref>{{cite web |title=Indoor Air Comfort |url=http://www.indoor-air-comfort.com/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110201124732/http://www.indoor-air-comfort.com/ |archive-date=February 1, 2011 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Indoor Air Comfort |url-status=live }}</ref> in Europe, as well as California Standard CDPH Section 01350<ref>{{cite web |title=CDPH Section 01350 |url=http://www.eurofins.com/section-1350.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924003428/http://www.eurofins.com/section-1350.aspx |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=March 2, 2012 |publisher=Eurofins.com }}</ref> and several others in the US. Due to these initiatives an increasing number of low-emitting products became available to purchase.

At least 18 microbial VOCs (MVOCs) have been characterized<ref name="smell-2021">{{cite web |title=Smelly Moldy Houses |url=http://www.bioidea.net/resources/smelly-musty-moldy-houses/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215040749/https://www.bioidea.net/resources/smelly-musty-moldy-houses/ |archive-date=December 15, 2021 |access-date=August 2, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Meruva |first1=N. K. |last2=Penn |first2=J. M. |last3=Farthing |first3=D. E. |date=November 2004 |title=Rapid identification of microbial VOCs from tobacco molds using closed-loop stripping and gas chromatography/time-of-flight mass spectrometry |journal=J Ind Microbiol Biotechnol |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=482–8 |doi=10.1007/s10295-004-0175-0 |pmid=15517467 |s2cid=32543591 |doi-access=free }}</ref> including [[1-octen-3-ol]] (mushroom alcohol), [[3-Methylfuran]], [[2-pentanol]], [[2-hexanone]], [[2-heptanone]], [[3-octanone]], [[3-octanol]], [[2-octen-1-ol]], [[1-octene]], [[2-pentanone]], [[2-nonanone]], [[borneol]], [[geosmin]], [[1-butanol]], [[3-methyl-1-butanol]], [[3-methyl-2-butanol]], and [[thujopsene]]. The last four are products of ''[[Stachybotrys chartarum]]'', which has been linked with [[sick building syndrome]].<ref name="smell-2021" />

==== Asbestos fibers ====

Many common building materials (especially those manufactured in the United States before 1976)<ref>{{cite news |last1=Guillén |first1=Alex |title=EPA moves to ban asbestos after decades of failures |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/04/05/epa-moves-ban-asbestos-00022900 |access-date=20 November 2025 |work=POLITICO |date=5 April 2022 |language=en }}</ref> contain [[asbestos]], such as some floor tiles, ceiling tiles, shingles, fireproofing, heating systems, pipe wrap, taping muds, mastics, and other insulation materials. Normally, significant releases of asbestos fiber do not occur unless the building materials are disturbed, such as by cutting, sanding, drilling, or building remodeling. Removal of asbestos-containing materials is not always optimal because the fibers can be spread into the air during the removal process. A management program for intact asbestos-containing materials is often recommended instead.

When asbestos-containing material is damaged or disintegrates, microscopic fibers are dispersed into the air. Inhalation of asbestos fibers over long exposure times is associated with increased incidence of [[lung cancer]], [[mesothelioma]], and [[asbestosis]]. The risk of lung cancer from inhaling asbestos fibers is significantly greater for smokers. The symptoms of disease do not usually appear until about 20 to 30 years after the first exposure to asbestos.

Although all asbestos is hazardous, products that are friable, e.g. sprayed coatings and insulation, pose a significantly higher hazard as they are more likely to release fibers to the air.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2016 |title=Atmospheric carbon dioxide passes 400 ppm everywhere |journal=Physics Today |issue=6 |article-number=8170 |doi=10.1063/pt.5.029904|bibcode=2016PhT..2016f8170. }}</ref>

==== Ozone ====

{{See also|Ground-level ozone}}
Indoors [[ozone]] (O<sub>3</sub>) is produced by certain [[High voltage|high-voltage]] electric devices (such as [[air ionizer]]s), and as a by-product of other types of pollution. It appears in lower concentrations indoors than outdoors, usually at 0.2–0.7 of the outdoor concentration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Weschler |first=Charles J. |date=December 2000 |title=Ozone in Indoor Environments: Concentration and Chemistry: Ozone in Indoor Environments |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1034/j.1600-0668.2000.010004269.x |url-status=live |journal=Indoor Air |language=en |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=269–288 |doi=10.1034/j.1600-0668.2000.010004269.x |pmid=11089331 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240415110851/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1034/j.1600-0668.2000.010004269.x |archive-date=April 15, 2024 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Typically, most ozone is lost to surface reactions indoors, rather than to reactions in air, due to the large surface to volume ratios found indoors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Weschler |first1=Charles J. |last2=Nazaroff |first2=William W |date=February 22, 2023 |title=Human skin oil: a major ozone reactant indoors |journal=Environmental Science: Atmospheres |language=en |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=640–661 |doi=10.1039/D3EA00008G |issn=2634-3606 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2023ESAt....3..640W }}</ref>

Outdoor air used for ventilation may have sufficient ozone to react with common indoor pollutants as well as skin oils and other common indoor air chemicals or surfaces. Particular concern is warranted when using "green" cleaning products based on citrus or terpene extracts, because these chemicals react rapidly with ozone to form toxic and irritating chemicals<ref name="pmid38258874" /> as well as [[Atmospheric particulate matter|fine]] and [[ultrafine particles]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Prashant |last2=Kalaiarasan |first2=Gopinath |last3=Porter |first3=Alexandra E. |last4=Pinna |first4=Alessandra |last5=Kłosowski |first5=Michał M. |last6=Demokritou |first6=Philip |last7=Chung |first7=Kian Fan |author-link7=Kian F. Chung |last8=Pain |first8=Christopher |last9=Arvind |first9=D. K. |last10=Arcucci |first10=Rossella |last11=Adcock |first11=Ian M. |last12=Dilliway |first12=Claire |date=February 20, 2021 |title=An overview of methods of fine and ultrafine particle collection for physicochemical characterisation and toxicity assessments |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=756 |article-number=143553 |bibcode=2021ScTEn.75643553K |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.143553 |pmid=33239200 |s2cid=227176222 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=10044/1/84518 }}</ref>  Ventilation with outdoor air containing elevated ozone concentrations may complicate remediation attempts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Apte |first1=M. G. |last2=Buchanan |first2=I. S. H. |last3=Mendell |first3=M. J. |date=April 2008 |title=Outdoor ozone and building-related symptoms in the BASE study |journal=Indoor Air |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=156–170 |bibcode=2008InAir..18..156A |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0668.2008.00521.x |pmid=18333994 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The WHO standard for ozone concentration is 60 μg/m<sup>3</sup> for long-term exposure and 100  μg/m<sup>3</sup> as the maximum average over an 8-hour period.<ref name=":2" /> The EPA standard for ozone concentration is 0.07 ppm average over an 8-hour period.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eight-hour Average Ozone Concentrations {{!}} Ground-level Ozone {{!}} New England {{!}} US EPA |url=https://www3.epa.gov/region1/airquality/avg8hr.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211215040747/https://www3.epa.gov/region1/airquality/avg8hr.html |archive-date=December 15, 2021 |access-date=September 16, 2019 |website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] |language=en }}</ref>

=== Biological agents ===

==== Mold and other allergens ====
{{Main|Indoor mold|Mold health issues}}

Occupants in buildings can be exposed to fungal spores, cell fragments, or [[mycotoxin]]s which can arise from a host of means, but there are two common classes: (a) excess moisture induced growth of [[mold]] colonies and (b) natural substances released into the air such as animal dander and plant pollen.<ref name="pmid21196349">{{cite journal |last1=Park |first1=J. H. |last2=Cox-Ganser |first2=J. M. |year=2011 |title=Meta-Mold exposure and respiratory health in damp indoor environments |journal=[[Frontiers in Bioscience]] |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=757–771 |doi=10.2741/e284 |pmid=21196349 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

While mold growth is associated with high moisture levels,<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 4, 2018 |title=CDC – Mold – General Information – Facts About Mold and Dampness |url=https://www.cdc.gov/mold/dampness_facts.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191216124251/https://www.cdc.gov/mold/dampness_facts.htm |archive-date=December 16, 2019 |access-date=June 23, 2017 }}</ref> it is likely to grow when a combination of favorable conditions arises. As well as high moisture levels, these conditions include suitable temperatures, [[pH]] and nutrient sources.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9781135824624 |title=Building Mycology |publisher=Taylor & Francis |year=1994 |isbn=978-1-135-82462-4 |editor-last=Singh |editor-first=Dr Jagjit |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.4324/9780203974735 |editor-last2=Singh |editor-first2=Jagjit }}</ref> Mold grows primarily on surfaces,&nbsp;and it reproduces by releasing spores, which can travel and settle in different locations. When these spores experience appropriate conditions, they can germinate and lead to [[mycelium]] growth.<ref name="Clarke-1999">{{Cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=J.A |last2=Johnstone |first2=C.M |last3=Kelly |first3=N.J |last4=McLean |first4=R.C |last5=anderson |first5=J.A |last6=Rowan |first6=N.J |last7=Smith |first7=J.E |date=January 20, 1999 |title=A technique for the prediction of the conditions leading to mould growth in buildings |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0360132398000237 |url-status=live |journal=Building and Environment |language=en |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=515–521 |bibcode=1999BuEnv..34..515C |doi=10.1016/S0360-1323(98)00023-7 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221026052956/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0360132398000237 |archive-date=October 26, 2022 |access-date=April 10, 2024 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Different mold species favor different environmental conditions to germinate and grow, some being more [[Hydrophile|hydrophilic]] (growing at higher levels of relative humidity) and other more [[Xerophile|xerophilic]] (growing at levels of relative humidity as low as 75–80%).<ref name="Clarke-1999" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vereecken |first1=Evy |last2=Roels |first2=Staf |date=November 15, 2011 |title=Review of mould prediction models and their influence on mould risk evaluation |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0360132311003830 |url-status=live |journal=Building and Environment |language=en |volume=51 |pages=296–310 |doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2011.11.003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240302035904/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0360132311003830 |archive-date=March 2, 2024 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Mold growth can be inhibited by keeping surfaces at conditions that are further from condensation, with relative humidity levels below 75%. This usually translates to a relative humidity of indoor air below 60%, in agreement with the guidelines for thermal comfort that recommend a relative humidity between 40 and 60%. Moisture buildup in buildings may arise from water penetrating areas of the [[building envelope]] or fabric, from plumbing leaks, rainwater or groundwater penetration, or from [[condensation]] due to improper ventilation, insufficient heating or poor thermal quality of the building envelope.<ref>{{Cite book |title=BS 5250:2021 - Management of moisture in buildings. Code of practice |date=October 31, 2021 |publisher=British Standards Institution (BSI) |isbn=978-0-539-18975-9 }}</ref> Even something as simple as drying clothes indoors on [[Radiator (heating)|radiators]] can increase the risk of mold growth, if the humidity produced is not able to escape the building via ventilation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Madgwick |first1=Della |last2=Wood |first2=Hannah |date=August 8, 2016 |title=The problem of clothes drying in new homes in the UK |url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048/full/html |url-status=live |journal=Structural Survey |language=en |volume=34 |issue=4/5 |pages=320–330 |doi=10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048 |issn=0263-080X |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507231216/https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/SS-10-2015-0048/full/html |archive-date=May 7, 2021 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Mold predominantly affects the airways and lungs. Known effects of mold on health include [[asthma]] development and exacerbation,<ref>{{Cite web |last1=May |first1=Neil |last2=McGilligan |first2=Charles |last3=Ucci |first3=Marcella |date=2017 |title=Health and Moisture in Buildings |url=https://ukcmb.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/health-and-moisture-in-buildings-report-1.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240411070746/https://ukcmb.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/health-and-moisture-in-buildings-report-1.pdf |archive-date=April 11, 2024 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |website=UK Centre for Moisture in Buildings }}</ref> with children and elderly at greater risk of more severe health impacts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 7, 2023 |title=Understanding and addressing the health risks of damp and mould in the home |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/damp-and-mould-understanding-and-addressing-the-health-risks-for-rented-housing-providers/understanding-and-addressing-the-health-risks-of-damp-and-mould-in-the-home--2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240410023335/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/damp-and-mould-understanding-and-addressing-the-health-risks-for-rented-housing-providers/understanding-and-addressing-the-health-risks-of-damp-and-mould-in-the-home--2 |archive-date=April 10, 2024 |access-date=April 11, 2024 |website=GOV.UK |language=en }}</ref> Infants in homes with mold have a much greater risk of developing [[asthma]] and [[allergic rhinitis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Sierra N. |last2=Lam |first2=Holly C. Y. |last3=Goode |first3=Emma-Jane |last4=Marczylo |first4=Emma L. |last5=Exley |first5=Karen S. |last6=Dimitroulopoulou |first6=Sani |date=2023-08-02 |title=The Burden of Respiratory Disease from Formaldehyde, Damp and Mould in English Housing |journal=Environments |language=en |volume=10 |issue=8 |page=136 |doi=10.3390/environments10080136 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023Envi...10..136C |issn=2076-3298 }}</ref><ref name="pmid21196349" /> More than half of adult workers in moldy or humid buildings suffer from nasal or sinus symptoms due to mold exposure.<ref name="pmid21196349" /> Some varieties of mold contain toxic compounds ([[mycotoxin]]s). However, exposure to hazardous levels of mycotoxin via inhalation is not possible in most cases, as toxins are produced by the fungal body and are not at significant levels in the released spores.

==== ''Legionella'' ====

{{unreferenced section|date=September 2024}}
[[Legionnaires' disease]] is caused by a waterborne bacterium ''[[Legionella]]'' that grows best in slow-moving or still, warm water. The primary route of exposure is through the creation of an aerosol effect, most commonly from evaporative cooling towers or showerheads.<ref>{{cite web |title=Legionella (Legionnaires' Disease and Pontiac Fever) |date=August 6, 2025 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/legionella/ |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |access-date=2026-05-04 }}</ref> A common source of ''Legionella'' in commercial buildings is from poorly placed or maintained evaporative cooling towers, which often release water in an aerosol which may enter nearby ventilation intakes. Outbreaks in medical facilities and nursing homes, where patients are [[Immunosuppression|immuno-suppressed]] and immuno-weak, are the most commonly reported cases of Legionellosis. More than one case has involved outdoor fountains at public attractions. The presence of ''Legionella'' in commercial building water supplies is highly underreported, as healthy people require heavy exposure to acquire infection.

''Legionella'' testing typically involves collecting water samples and surface swabs from evaporative cooling basins, shower heads, faucets/taps, and other locations where warm water collects. The samples are then cultured and [[Colony-forming unit|colony forming units]] (cfu) of Legionella are quantified as cfu/liter.

''Legionella'' is a parasite of [[protozoa]]ns such as [[amoeba]], and thus requires conditions suitable for both organisms. The bacterium forms a [[biofilm]] which is resistant to chemical and antimicrobial treatments, including chlorine. Remediation for ''Legionella'' outbreaks in commercial buildings vary, but often include hot water flushes ({{convert|160|F|C}}), sterilisation of standing water in evaporative cooling basins, replacement of shower heads, and, in some cases, flushes of heavy metal salts. Preventive measures include adjusting normal hot water levels to allow for {{Convert|120|F|C}} at the tap, evaluating facility design layout, removing [[faucet aerator]]s, and periodic testing in suspect areas.

==== Other bacteria ====

[[File:Bacteria (26 2 27) Airborne microbes.jpg|thumb|Airborne bacteria]]

There are many [[bacteria]] of health significance found in indoor air and on indoor surfaces. The role of microbes in the indoor environment is increasingly studied using modern gene-based analysis of environmental samples. Currently, efforts are under way to link microbial ecologists and indoor air scientists to forge new methods for analysis and to better interpret the results.<ref>[http://www.microbe.net/ Microbiology of the Indoor Environment] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723210118/http://www.microbe.net/ |date=July 23, 2011 }}, microbe.net</ref>

A large fraction of the bacteria found in indoor air and dust are shed from humans. Among the most important bacteria known to occur in indoor air are [[Mycobacterium tuberculosis]], [[Staphylococcus aureus]], [[Streptococcus pneumoniae]].{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

==== Virus ====

[[File:Hotel Metropole 9th floor layout SARS 2003.svg|thumbnail|Ninth floor layout of the Metropole Hotel in Hong Kong, showing where an outbreak of the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) occurred]]

Viruses can also be a concern for indoor air quality. During the [[2002–2004 SARS outbreak]], virus-laden aerosols were found to have seeped into bathrooms from the bathroom floor drains, exacerbated by the draw of bathroom exhaust fans, resulting in the rapid spread of SARS in [[Amoy Gardens#SARS outbreak|Amoy Gardens]] in [[Hong Kong]].<ref>{{Cite web| title=Outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) at Amoy Gardens, Kowloon Bay, Hong Kong - Main Findings of the Investigation |url=http://www.info.gov.hk/info/sars/pdf/amoy_e.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930041836/http://www.info.gov.hk/info/sars/pdf/amoy_e.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-30 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Floor Drains at Amoy Gardens |url=https://www.info.gov.hk/info/sars/graphics/amoyannex.jpg |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180616192315/http://www.info.gov.hk/info/sars/graphics/amoyannex.jpg | archive-date=2018-06-16 }}</ref> Elsewhere in Hong Kong, SARS CoV RNA was found on the carpet and in the [[air intake]] vents of the Metropole Hotel, which showed that secondary environmental contamination could generate [[Aerosol|infectious aerosols]] and resulted in superspreading events.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Braden |first1=Christopher R. |last2=Dowell |first2=Scott F. |last3=Jernigan |first3=Daniel B. |last4=Hughes |first4=James M. |url=https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/19/6/13-0192_article|quote=environmental contamination with SARS CoV RNA was identified on the carpet in front of the index case-patient's room and 3 nearby rooms (and on their door frames but not inside the rooms) and in the air intake vents near the centrally located elevators ... secondary infections occurred not in guest rooms but in the common areas of the ninth floor, such as the corridor or elevator hall. These areas could have been contaminated through body fluids (e.g., vomitus, expectorated sputum), respiratory droplets, or suspended small-particle aerosols generated by the index case-patient; other guests were then infected by fomites or aerosols while passing through these same areas. Efficient spread of SARS CoV through small-particle aerosols was observed in several superspreading events in health care settings, during an airplane flight, and in an apartment complex (12–14,16–19). This process of environmental contamination that generated infectious aerosols likely best explains the pattern of disease transmission at the Hotel Metropole.|title=Progress in Global Surveillance and Response Capacity 10 Years after Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome |journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases |date=2013 |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=864–869 |doi=10.3201/eid1906.130192 |pmid=23731871 |pmc=3713843 }}</ref>

===Carbon dioxide===

Humans are the main indoor source of [[carbon dioxide]] (CO<sub>2</sub>) in most occupied buildings. Indoor CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations can be used as an indicator of the adequacy of outdoor air ventilation relative to occupancy and metabolic activity.

Exposure to elevated indoor CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations has been investigated in relation to human health and cognitive performance. Some studies have reported physiological and psychomotor effects at relatively low concentrations, although the evidence is not consistent and it can be difficult to distinguish the effects of CO<sub>2</sub> itself from those of other pollutants and human bioeffluents associated with inadequate ventilation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Azuma |first1=Kenichi |last2=Kagi |first2=Naoki |last3=Yanagi |first3=U. |last4=Osawa |first4=Haruki |title=Effects of low-level inhalation exposure to carbon dioxide in indoor environments: A short review on human health and psychomotor performance |journal=Environment International |date=December 2018 |volume=121 |issue=Pt 1 |pages=51–56 |doi=10.1016/j.envint.2018.08.059 |pmid=30172928 |bibcode=2018EnInt.121...51A |doi-access=free }}</ref> Reviews of the available evidence have reported possible effects on cognitive performance at concentrations above 1000 ppm, particularly during complex tasks, although the evidence remains subject to uncertainty.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Du |first1=Bowen |last2=Tandoc |first2=Michael |date=June 19, 2020 |title=Indoor CO2 concentrations and cognitive function: A critical review |journal=International Journal of Indoor Environment and Health |volume=30 |issue=6 |pages=1067–1082 |bibcode=2020InAir..30.1067D |doi=10.1111/ina.12706 |pmid=32557862 |s2cid=219915861 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=Yuejie |last2=Cao |first2=Xiaodong |last3=Zhang |first3=Jie |last4=Lai |first4=Dayi |last5=Pang |first5=Liping |date=June 1, 2023 |title=Short-term exposure to indoor carbon dioxide and cognitive task performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Building and Environment |language=en |volume=237 |article-number=110331 |bibcode=2023BuEnv.23710331F |doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2023.110331 |doi-access=free }}</ref> At concentrations below 5000 ppm, the health effects attributable specifically to CO<sub>2</sub> are difficult to distinguish from those associated with other indoor pollutants and inadequate ventilation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Lowther |first1=Scott D. |last2=Dimitroulopoulou |first2=Sani |last3=Foxall |first3=Kerry |last4=Shrubsole |first4=Clive |last5=Cheek |first5=Emily |last6=Gadeberg |first6=Britta |last7=Sepai |first7=Ovnair |date=16 November 2021 |title=Low Level Carbon Dioxide Indoors—A Pollution Indicator or a Pollutant? A Health-Based Perspective |journal=Environments |language=en |volume=8 |issue=11 |page=125 |doi=10.3390/environments8110125 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021Envi....8..125L |issn=2076-3298 }}</ref>

Indoor CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations are widely used as an indicator of ventilation performance in buildings.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Persily |first1=Andrew |title=Development and application of an indoor carbon dioxide metric |journal=Indoor Air |date=July 2022 |volume=32 |issue=7 |article-number=e13059 |doi=10.1111/ina.13059 |doi-access=free |pmid=35904382 |bibcode=2022InAir..3213059P }}</ref> Because indoor concentrations are influenced by occupancy, ventilation rates, building characteristics and outdoor conditions, measurements of CO<sub>2</sub> can provide information on the adequacy of air exchange in occupied spaces. Harmonized analyses of measurements from residential buildings have shown substantial variation in indoor CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations according to ventilation type and other building and environmental characteristics.<ref name="Rojas2026">{{cite journal
|last1=Rojas
|first1=Gabriel
|last2=Stauffer
|first2=Reto
|last3=Casquero-Modrego
|first3=Núria
|last4=Loomans
|first4=Marcel
|last5=Abadie
|first5=Marc
|title=Towards a harmonized database of indoor air contaminant concentrations: Methods and application to CO2
|journal=Building and Environment
|date=2026
|volume=292
|article-number=114297
|issn=0360-1323
|doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2026.114297
|doi-access=free
|hdl=10261/419764
|hdl-access=free
}}</ref>

Guidelines and standards use CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations as an indicator of indoor air quality and ventilation. The [[National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health]] (NIOSH) considers concentrations above 1000 ppm to be a marker suggesting inadequate ventilation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Indoor Environmental Quality: Building Ventilation |url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/indoorenv/BuildingVentilation.html |access-date=October 8, 2008 |website=National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health |language=en}}</ref> Guidance for schools in the United Kingdom has used concentrations of 800 ppm or lower as an indicator of good ventilation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SAMHE - Schools' Air quality Monitoring for Health and Education |url=https://samhe.org.uk/resources/samhe.org.uk |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=samhe.org.uk |language=en |archive-date=March 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240318200228/https://samhe.org.uk/resources/samhe.org.uk |url-status=live }}</ref> Thresholds used to characterize indoor air quality vary among standards and guidance documents.<ref name=":3" />

In occupied, poorly ventilated spaces, CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations can rise substantially above outdoor levels within a relatively short period. The rate of increase depends on factors such as room volume, occupancy and ventilation. Measurements in enclosed office spaces have shown that concentrations can rise from approximately 500 ppm to above 1000 ppm within tens of minutes after ventilation is stopped.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Document Display |url=https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyNET.exe/00000AOV.TXT?ZyActionD=ZyDocument&Client=EPA&Index=1991+Thru+1994&Docs=&Query=&Time=&EndTime=&SearchMethod=1&TocRestrict=n&Toc=&TocEntry=&QField=&QFieldYear=&QFieldMonth=&QFieldDay=&IntQFieldOp=0&ExtQFieldOp=0&XmlQuery=&File=D:%5Czyfiles%5CIndex%20Data%5C91thru94%5CTxt%5C00000009%5C00000AOV.txt&User=ANONYMOUS&Password=anonymous&SortMethod=h%7C-&MaximumDocuments=1&FuzzyDegree=0&ImageQuality=r75g8/r75g8/x150y150g16/i425&Display=hpfr&DefSeekPage=ZyActionL&Back=ZyActionS&BackDesc=Results&MaximumPages=1&ZyEntry=1&SeekPage=x&ZyPURL |access-date=October 19, 2023 |website=NEPIS |language=en}}</ref>

=== Radon ===
{{Main|Radon}}

[[Radon]] is an invisible, radioactive atomic gas that results from the radioactive decay of [[radium]], which may be found in rock formations beneath buildings or in certain building materials themselves.

Radon is probably the most pervasive serious hazard for indoor air in the United States and Europe. It is a major cause of [[lung cancer]], responsible for 3–14% of cases in countries, leading to tens of thousands of deaths.{{sfn|Zeeb|Shannoun|2009|p=3}}

Radon gas enters buildings as a [[soil gas]]. As it is a heavy gas it will tend to accumulate at the lowest level. Radon may also be introduced into a building through drinking water particularly from bathroom showers. Building materials can be a rare source of radon, but little testing is carried out for stone, rock or tile products brought into building sites; radon accumulation is greatest for well insulated homes.<ref>C.Michael Hogan and Sjaak Slanina. 2010, [http://www.eoearth.org/ ''Air pollution''. Encyclopedia of Earth] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061012144354/http://www.eoearth.org/|date=October 12, 2006}}. eds. Sidney Draggan and Cutler Cleveland. National Council for Science and the Environment. Washington DC.</ref> There are simple do-it-yourself kits for radon gas testing, but a licensed professional can also check homes.

The [[half-life]] for radon is 3.8 days, indicating that once the source is removed, the hazard will be greatly reduced within a few weeks. [[Radon mitigation]] methods include sealing concrete slab floors, basement foundations, water drainage systems, or by increasing [[cross ventilation|ventilation]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OAR |date=2014-07-29 |title=Air Cleaners and Air Filters in the Home |url=https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/air-cleaners-and-air-filters-home |access-date=2026-09-18 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Radon Mitigation Methods |url=http://radon-solution.com/pg_mitigation_methods.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081215190050/http://radon-solution.com/pg_mitigation_methods.php |archive-date=December 15, 2008 |access-date=December 2, 2008 |publisher=Radon Solution—Raising Radon Awareness }}</ref> They are usually cost effective and can greatly reduce or even eliminate the contamination and the associated health risks.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

Radon is measured in [[Curie (unit)|picocuries]] per liter of air (pCi/L) or [[becquerel]] per cubic meter (Bq m<sup>-3)</sup>. Both are measurements of radioactivity. The [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) sets the ideal indoor radon levels at 100 Bq/m-<sup>3</sup>.{{sfn|Zeeb|Shannoun|2009|p={{page needed|date=March 2024}}}} In the United States, it is recommend to fix homes with radon levels at or above 4 pCi/L. At the same time it is also recommends that people think about fixing their homes for radon levels between 2 pCi/L and 4 pCi/L.<ref>{{cite web |title=Basic radon facts |url=https://www.wvdhhr.org/rtia/pdf/Radon%20Facts.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220113132625/https://www.wvdhhr.org/RTIA/pdf/Radon%20Facts.pdf |archive-date=January 13, 2022 |access-date=September 18, 2018 |publisher=US Environmental Protection Agency |language=en}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> In the United Kingdom the ideal is presence of radon indoors is 100 Bq/m-<sup>3</sup>. Action needs to be taken in homes with 200 Bq/m<sup>−3</sup> or more.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Radon Action Level and Target Level |url=https://www.ukradon.org/information/level |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240318160250/https://www.ukradon.org/information/level |archive-date=March 18, 2024 |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=UKradon }}</ref>

Interactive maps of radon affected areas are available for various regions and countries of the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Radon Zone Map (with State Information) |url=https://gispub.epa.gov/radon/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401042017/https://gispub.epa.gov/radon/ |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=April 10, 2024 |website=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=UK maps of radon |url=https://www.ukradon.org/information/ukmaps |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240307083700/https://www.ukradon.org/information/ukmaps |archive-date=March 7, 2024 |access-date=April 10, 2024 |website=UKradon }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Radon map of Australia |url=https://www.arpansa.gov.au/understanding-radiation/radiation-sources/more-radiation-sources/radon-map |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240320110315/https://www.arpansa.gov.au/understanding-radiation/radiation-sources/more-radiation-sources/radon-map |archive-date=March 20, 2024 |access-date=April 10, 2024 |website=Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA) }}</ref>

== IAQ and climate change ==

{{See also|Effects of climate change on human health}}
Indoor air quality is linked inextricably to [[Air pollution|outdoor air quality]]. The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) has varying scenarios that predict how the climate will change in the future.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science
